author: Abahlali_3
title: This August we honour the women of South Africa
content:
11 August 2026 Abahlali baseMjondolo Press Statement

This August we honour the women of South Africa

This August, in women’s month, we speak of the comrades who are mothers, daughters, sisters and grandmothers, comrades who wake up every morning in the shack settlements and carry the weight of a country that has forgotten them.

We honour the women who keep their families going under conditions of brutal impoverishment and the women who resist oppression. We honour the women in our movement.

But this is not a month of celebration.

No woman is fully free in South Africa. All women are at risk of violence. Impoverished women remain profoundly oppressed.

There is no celebration when women continue to live under very dangerous conditions.

There is no celebration when a woman must walk to a communal tap after dark and risk rape or attack.

There is no celebration when there is no electricity, no running water, no toilets, and no safety for children.

There is no celebration when a woman does not know if her home will be standing tomorrow because of evictions, fires, or political violence.

For millions of impoverished women in shacks, tin houses and backyards, every day is a fight for survival.

To celebrate while all this is true is to lie.

This August we honour all the women of our movement who refused to accept poverty as fate.

We honour Nqobile Nzuza who was murdered by a police officer on a road blockade in Cato Crest on 30 September 2013. She was seventeen years old and doing her matric. She joined the road blockade in protest against the brutal attacks on the Marikana Land Occupation in Cato Manor by the eThekwini Municipality. She was committed to the struggle for land.

We honour Comrade Thuli Ndlovu, a leader of Abahlali baseMjondolo in KwaNdengezi. She fought for land, for housing, and for the dignity of her community. She was assassinated on 27 September 2014 for confronting oppression.

We honour Comrade Nokuthula Mabaso, a leader of eKhenana Commune and of the Abahlali Women’s League. She was a mother, an organiser, and a builder of a community that fed itself and governed itself. She was assassinated on 5 May 2022 while her community was under attack. She knew that poor people must seize the right to land and to live with dignity.

Our brave comrades refused oppression and insisted on land and dignity. Thuli and Nokuthula were leaders.

We also honour other women who have given their lives in the struggle for justice.

Fikile Ntshangase was a leading member of the Mfolozi Community Environmental Justice Organisation (MCEJO) which opposed the destruction of people’s land and homes by coal mining. She was assassinated on 22 October 2020.

Babita Deokaran was an honest civil servant and a whistleblower in the Gauteng Department of Health. She exposed corruption and the theft of public money meant for the public hospitals and clinics that serve the poor. She was assassinated in 2021 for refusing to look away as powerful and dangerous men looted the healthcare system.

We have no interest in politicians who come with speeches and flowers and say nothing about the oppression we live today and nothing about our leaders who have given their lives in the struggle against this oppression.

1.⁠ ⁠Secure access to land and decent housing so no woman sleeps in fear of eviction or fire. 2.⁠ Access to basic services such as water, electricity, sanitation, and safe public lighting in every settlement. 3.⁠ ⁠An end to political killings and intimidation of women organisers. 4.⁠ ⁠An end to gender-based violence in homes, streets, schools and communities. 5.⁠ ⁠Decent work, healthcare and education so women are not forced to choose between feeding their children and their own health. 6. Reproductive healthcare and contraception available without humiliation or delay. 7. A livable guaranteed income in recognition of the unpaid care work that holds families and communities together. 8. Decisive action to reduce food prices on essential items. 9. An end to attempts to turn poor women against migrant and refugee women, since the enemy is landlessness, unemployment and state neglect, not our neighbours. 10.⁠ ⁠Accountability for the killings of Nqobile, Thuli, Nokuthula, Fikile, Babita and all the other murdered and assassinated women activists whose cases were closed and forgotten.

Poor women are not asking to be celebrated. We are demanding to be safe, to be housed, to be heard, to be alive.

Until that happens, August …

author: William Shoki
title: On Safari
content:
Ever since the

World Cup

 concluded with Spain’s emphatic triumph over universally loathed Argentina (at least it felt this way), it has no longer felt like everyone is looking in the same direction at the same time. For a month and a bit, football’s biggest stage gave us one of the last remaining experiences of shared, global time. Not global justice, not global equality — the tournament is in many ways a monument to their absence — but a crude, synchronized schedule. Games at set hours, short-lived solidarities, the impression, however false, that the world is briefly doing something together, undergoing a collective experience.

Once that all ends, you’re plunged back into a social temporality and news cycle that moves at lightning speed and adjusting back is disorienting. It didn’t help that I had to deal with a debilitating case of

cyclosporiasis

 (in an ill-fated decision, I tried some Taco Bell for the first time the day before my return flight back to South Africa, and getting a food-borne illness felt like an appropriate parting gift from a United States in decline). In the weeks since the World Cup, I found myself in a kind of fog I at first attributed to being exhausted from a busy year coupled with bouts of illness, but which, as I return to relatively decent health, I recognize as a familiar feeling, one that has typified contemporary experience for as long as I can remember.

There’s a book by the Polish sociologist Zygmunt Bauman which I think is underrated, and does better at capturing the texture of our epoch than many other attempts (do we live in late capitalism, surveillance capitalism, the burnout society, post-modernity, etc etc.). It’s called

Liquid Modernity

, and Bauman’s straightforward argument is that the defining feature of contemporary society is no longer the construction of stable institutions, identities, and social relationships, but their constant dissolution. Where the “solid” phase of modernity sought to build enduring structures — stable careers, lifelong marriages, nation-states, political parties, class identities, and fixed moral frameworks — our present condition is “liquid”: forms no longer retain their shape for long enough to organize human life. The contradictory result of this is that even though in many important respects, individuals have unprecedented freedom (at least compared to any other point in human history), it’s coupled with chronic insecurity and the burden of constantly having to remake ourselves.

One of his most evocative concepts is the notion of pointillist time, which is “more prominent for its inconsistency and lack of cohesion than for its elements of continuity and consistency.” Time under liquid modernity is fragmented and disconnected, and rather than unfolding as a series of events with some relationship to each other, it is rather a series of “eternal instants.” It’s not hard work to see how this characterizes so much of algorithm-dominated society in general, and our media consumption in particular. If it wasn’t hard enough figuring out what producing any meaningful “content” takes in the attention economy, it was dismaying for me to recently learn that even new media like podcasts and video essays are themselves now being repurposed in a

“clipping economy”

 where increasingly, circulation of short clips from longer pieces is becoming the main event rather than previews.

At

Africa Is a Country

, we are very proud of our World Cup Road Trip series. Three episodes are live —

Episode 1

 on the Cabo Verdean diaspora in New England,

Episode 2

 on the affinity between Algeria and Lawrence, Kansas, and

Episode 3

 on Toronto’s Ghanaian community — with further episodes from the road currently in post-production. Although the website and our weekly newsletters remain our bread and butter, like most outlets, we are experimenting with different ways of reaching audiences, and short-form video has been one of them. The newsletter in particular functions as our most reliable direct channel to readers as social platform referrals grow less dependable. The World Cup, however, gave us a powerful on-ramp: sport brought in readers who might not otherwise arrive at a piece on visa regimes or xenophobia, and the coverage was built to convert that interest into political understanding.

What has been challenging is that discovery is now heavily platform-dependent, and the same work travels very differently depending on where it lands: our road trip …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Senegal’s World Cup Exit: The Price of National Honor and Women’s Safety
content:
The reigning African champions were eliminated from the 2026 FIFA World Cup on 1 July, beaten 3-2 by Belgium in extra time in the Round of 32. The Lions of Teranga had gone two goals up early, lifting hopes across the country and the continent, before Belgium’s comeback sent them home. What has followed is a dramatic unfolding of events that expose the disturbing and persistent patterns beyond the Senegalese team. 


During the tournament, players were reportedly seen ordering food outside their designated hotel. The detail seemed trivial until it emerged that the team’s chef was not with the squad at all. The Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) initially pointed to visa problems, easy to accept given the treatment African teams and supporters have received from the United States and Canada as hosts. 


But as scrutiny mounted, a different account surfaced. More than ten days after the defeat, the federation’s general secretary, Abdoulaye Seydou Sow, appeared on the Senegalese public broadcaster RTS on

Sunday, July 12

and confirmed what social media had reported: the chef had been accused of sexual harassment by an employee recruited in the United States. Faced with the allegations, Sow said, “the federation chose to act without delay.”

 

The chef was sent home. 


“Everyone should congratulate the federation president and me because we protected Senegal’s honor and dignity,” Sow said. “We did not want to make the matter public, but once we became aware of the facts and the procedures that could follow, we acted immediately.”


Keeping him on American soil, Sow explained, might have invited intervention by US authorities. The removal was a precaution: to preserve calm in the squad and keep the matter from disrupting Senegal’s campaign. He went further, noting that the secretary general also stressed that certain behaviors that might be perceived in Senegal as mere joking can, under American law, be considered harassment. That the federation had acted with caution to avoid potential legal or media consequences that might damage the image of the team and the country. He spoke with pride of a man who believed he had guarded Senegal’s “honor and dignity”.


At no time did the official go beyond reputational handling to address safeguarding. It is a reputational one. The complainant is entirely absent from the account: we are not told whether an investigation was opened, whether she was supported, or what became of her. The chef was moved out of American jurisdiction, and the country wasn’t told if he was still in a position of authority. The federation solved exposure, not harm.


Sexual harassment at the global stage


His words sparked immediate anger online, and rightly so. In distinguishing Senegalese joking from American law, he made consent a matter of geography. His words echo what we live every day. Ask any Senegalese woman, and she will give you an inventory: the sexist joke, the vulgar remark, the hand that lands on you in a crowded place, the man who does not ask because he has never had to. This is what we are told is culture. Men joke, men pat, men say things, and nothing about it is deemed inappropriate. 


The statement is as true as it is unflinching. It says out loud what is usually left implicit, and, in doing so, stamps society’s approval on it. What shocks is the casualness: that a man at that level would relay it to the nation as though we should carry on and accept it. To the man at the top of Senegalese football, he was standing up for his buddies and the nation’s collective pride, weighing both against a woman’s safety. He did not think to denounce sexual misconduct at all.


Sexual harassment violates human rights, yet the federation’s account makes no reference to the codes that bind it. Under


FIFA rules

, sexual abuse, harassment and exploitation are not subject to any limitation period, an acknowledgement that such cases often surface years later. So removing the alleged perpetrator from the scene doesn’t necessarily resolve the case. FIFA’s framework also requires member associations to appoint a safeguarding officer and maintain reporting channels for anyone working with, in, or around them. The FSF has not said whether it has either. Evading accountability in the name of the nation is the same instinct that drives the corruption and mismanagement dogging the FSF through this tournament.


Dakar street scene with a crowd celebrating and waving flags. Photo by

Felipe Esono Nguema …

author: Joseph Kayira
title: Malawi’s economic crisis: Can recovery begin?
content:
Almost nine months after Malawian President Peter Mutharika returned to power, his administration finds itself grappling with a severe and protracted economic crisis. The government faces the urgent challenge of restoring foreign exchange reserves, managing a growing external debt burden, reducing inflation and addressing chronic food insecurity.


When Malawi’s sixth president, Lazarus Chakwera, assumed office in 2020 after defeating Peter Mutharika in a

 court-ordered presidential election rerun,

 he pledged to rebuild the battered economy, create one million jobs for young people and root out systemic corruption in the civil service. His broader promises of wealth creation, entrepreneurship, good governance and food security, however, fell short of expectations.


By 2025, the election year, the

Tonse Alliance

 — a coalition of nine political parties — had effectively collapsed. Seven parties withdrew from the alliance, citing corruption, nepotism and a lack of clear policy direction within the Chakwera administration. The coalition had also been shaken by the death of Vice President Saulos Chilima in a plane crash in June 2024.


Underlying

c

auses of

e

conomic

d

ecline


As Chakwera’s term drew to a close, critics accused his administration of indecisiveness in the face of mounting economic challenges. Procurement scandals, allegations of nepotism and elite capture were widely cited as factors that allowed corruption to flourish, undermining efforts to stimulate economic growth.


The economy also suffered significant external shocks. Global supply chain disruptions following the Russia-Ukraine war drove up the cost of imports, while successive climate-related disasters devastated agricultural production.

Tropical Cyclone Freddy

 caused widespread flooding and mudslides that affected more than 2.2 million people in southern Malawi, compounding the country’s recovery from

Tropical Storm Ana

and

Tropical Cyclone Gombe.


Opposition parties, led by Mutharika’s Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), together with civil society organisations, criticised the Chakwera administration for excessive government spending, rising public debt and its handling of the International Monetary Fund’s Extended Credit Facility (ECF), which lapsed in May 2025.


In a statement issued on 16 May 2025, Reserve Bank of Malawi Governor Dr McDonald Mwale said: “The Reserve Bank of Malawi acknowledges the mutual decision by the Government and IMF to allow the ECF programme to lapse. This reflects ongoing fiscal and external challenges but does not signal a shift in Malawi’s commitment to sound macroeconomic management.”


On 9 November 2023, the Reserve Bank of Malawi announced a

 44 percent devaluation of the Malawi kwacha

. The central bank said the move was intended to allow the exchange rate to adjust to a market-clearing level and better reflect underlying market fundamentals.


Defending the decision, former Minister of Finance Simplex Chithyola argued that the overvalued kwacha had discouraged local production.


“If people find it cheaper to import goods than to buy locally produced products and services, it is a sign that the exchange rate is misaligned,” he said. “If this had continued, the long-term consequence would have been the collapse of local production and the transformation of Malawi into a dumping ground for cheap imported goods that add little value to our economy.”


Resuscitating the

‘

Sick

b

aby

’


Malawi’s President Peter Mutharika


Reviving the economy will be a formidable task. The Mutharika administration hopes to stabilise the kwacha, restore reliable supplies of fuel and foreign exchange, and create employment opportunities. Progress could be strengthened if negotiations with the IMF result in a new Extended Credit Facility programme.


Talks with an IMF delegation were scheduled for 9–18 June, with the Treasury indicating that it seeks support for its

National Economic Recovery Plan

without imposing reforms that would disproportionately burden ordinary Malawians.


A new agreement following the lapse of the four-year US$175 million ECF approved in November 2023 could restore donor confidence and support macroeconomic stability.


Finance Minister Joseph Mwanamvekha told

The Nation

 – a leading local daily – that government would only accept reforms that promote economic recovery while protecting vulnerable citizens.


“We will agree only to measures that help stabilise the economy …

author: Editor
title: Beyond Vision 2030: When Borrowed “Dreams” Meet a Venal Political Class
content:
A peculiar reflex in global development discourse: Whenever a leader in the developing world wants to signal ambition, competence, and modernity, they invoke Singapore. Rwanda’s Paul Kagame and, more recently, Kenya’s President

William Ruto

 have both held up the city-state as a model. In the run-up to the 2027 elections, Ruto has been telling Kenyans that he wants to transform the country into the “Singapore of Africa”. Singapore has thus become a kind of shorthand for the dream of rapid, state-led transformation. But what lies behind this obsession? Is it a serious policy blueprint, or simply a convenient slogan?


The fascination is continental. Kagame has called Singapore’s founding premier, Lee Kuan Yew, an inspiration, “

a great man… who achieved great things with a small country

”, and Rwanda is now routinely marketed as “the Singapore of Africa”. Ethiopia’s late Prime Minister Meles Zenawi built an entire ideology around the East Asian “developmental state”, and others have looked more loosely to the Asian Tigers as a template for leapfrogging the slow, contentious work of building democratic institutions.


The appeal is always the same: that a disciplined state, guided by capable technocrats and unburdened by messy pluralism, can compress decades of progress into a single generation. But the closer one looks at what the Singapore model demands, the more the dream complicates itself. Singapore’s story is indeed extraordinary. Expelled from Malaysia in 1965, it was a tiny island with no natural resources, high unemployment, and sharp ethnic tensions. Yet within a generation, it became one of the wealthiest nations on earth, with

per capita GDP

 surpassing that of most of Western Europe. Lee Kuan Yew’s formula was as much about incentives as ideals: to blunt the temptations of graft, he paid senior civil servants and ministers salaries that were competitive with those of the private sector, recruited ruthlessly on merit, and pursued corruption without regard to rank. Corruption today is virtually non-existent.


What made this possible? In his paper “

What is Governance?”

 Francis Fukuyama argues that government quality depends on the interaction of two dimensions: bureaucratic capacity and bureaucratic autonomy. Capacity refers to the resources and professionalization of a state’s institutions; autonomy denotes the insulation of the civil service from political micromanagement and patronage appointments. Neither dimension, on its own, is sufficient. Fukuyama explicitly places Singapore at the sweet spot of his governance matrix, combining high capacity with appropriate autonomy.


In contrast, Kenya occupies the

opposite corner

, characterized by low capacity and bureaucracies hollowed out by clientelism. Fukuyama adds a crucial insight: Singapore’s success rests as much on organizational culture as on formal rules. High-performing East Asian civil services are distinguished not only by correct procedures on paper, but by officials who have internalized professional norms. They are motivated, in his phrase, by social capital that promotes cooperative behaviour and substitutes for formal monitoring. Singapore built this culture deliberately, from the top down, over decades, not in a single electoral cycle.


The borrowing of models hasn’t stopped at the Strait of Malacca. On 8 July 2026, Ruto

signed the Sovereign Wealth Fund Act

 into law, ring-fencing 30 per cent of future petroleum and mineral revenues for an intergenerational “Urithi Fund”, alongside a stabilization buffer and infrastructure funds. The inspiration this time is Scandinavian. “We have borrowed heavily from Norway’s model,” Treasury Cabinet Secretary John Mbadi declared, while the president pointed to Norway’s fund, which he valued at roughly KSh280 trillion, and promised that Kenya too could reach first-world status within a generation. In a single news cycle, the national aspiration migrated from Singapore to Norway. But the underlying pattern is identical, and it is the pattern this essay is about: Kenya’s leaders keep importing the institutional artefacts of high-trust societies while leaving behind the trust that makes those artefacts work.


Norway’s

Government Pension Fund Global

 is indeed the gold standard, but its mechanics repay close attention, because everything Kenya is skipping lives in the details. Norway struck North Sea oil in 1969 and waited two decades before legislating the fund in 1990; the first deposit …

author: Amira El-Fekki
title: ‘Privacy chaos’: From fraudulent SIM registration to biometric data collection?
content:
A university student was sentenced last week to 25 years in prison, after a SIM card registered in his name was used in a drug-trafficking operation. He and his family have insisted that he never used the SIM card and had not even bought the card in the first place.


His case prompted many to check their own digital profiles and discover that dozens of phone numbers had been registered to their names without their knowledge.


In a wave of anger and concern about digital security, personal data security has become the topic of the hour as the scale of fraudulent phone line registration becomes clear.


The issue has been described as stemming from inadequate checks by mobile operators, who are supposed to demand passport or ID verification in person before allowing customers to establish a mobile phone number.


But permitting phone lines to be issued to customers showing digital copies of passports  leaves the door wide open to fraud, with commentators pointing to dozens of photographed IDs floating around digital platforms and messaging apps ripe for the taking.


The National Telecom Regulatory Authority has referred Egypt’s four mobile operators — Vodafone, Orange, e& and WE — to the Public Prosecution.


The NTRA has also proposed the introduction of biometric identity verification for the registration of new mobile network subscribers.


But why did the NTRA not detect or address the problem before it escalated? How are mobile companies held accountable for the data they collect and retain? 


And while steps have been taken to hold the companies legally responsible, is it enough to get to the root of the problem and ensure that biometric data handed to the NTRA will be handled securely?


The proposed biometric verification comes as Egypt’s personal data protection framework continues to face questions. Unlike data that can be changed, such as passwords, biometric data, such as facial scans, finger prints or eye scans, is permanently linked to the individual, and there is no going back if it is leaked. 


Its use across different services and platforms could also allow for the collection and collation of data belonging to the same person, to build an online data profile of them.


Mada Masr spoke to Mohamed al-Taher, the cofounder of and researcher with Masaar, an organization dedicated to digital rights and freedoms in Egypt, as well as Hassan al-Azhary, a lawyer and researcher with the organization, to unpack the implications of the NTRA’s decision. 


Azhary describes to Mada Masr the NTRA’s regulatory responsibilities and the legal ramifications of citizens discovering mobile lines registered in their names without their knowledge. He also talks us through data protection in Egypt and the loopholes in the regulatory framework and its enforcement. 


And Taher, meanwhile, points to the government’s inclination to begin using biometric data. 


Together, the pair express doubt as to whether biometric identity verification will solve the issue of fraudulent SIM card registration. Instead, they say, it could merely add another dimension to what they dub Egypt’s “privacy chaos.”


The interviews have been lightly edited for clarity.


Mada Masr:

The national regulator, the NTRA, said on Monday that it had referred Egypt’s four mobile operators to the Public Prosecution. Can we expect the referral to bring about better regulation and security in the handling of mobile data?


Hassan al-Azhary:

 The statement acknowledges that the incident is real, meaning there is a problem that concerns citizens complaining that lines have been registered in their names when they didn’t buy those lines.


SIM card distributors used to sell what were called “old” lines: there was this broad, vague and unclear discussion around the issue. This is the first clear and official acknowledgment that there is a problem.


Referring the matter to the Public Prosecution is important because it opens the door more broadly for affected citizens to start bringing lawsuits against the companies, depending on the harm they suffered. Some may seek compensation because they suffered direct harm. Others may seek compensation because they fear that they could be harmed, while some may seek to terminate their contracts. It depends on the extent of the harm each person has suffered.


The third point is that this referral shifts the matter from a question of administrative accountability to one of criminal accountability.

title: South Africans protest against xenophobia
content:
Thousands took to the streets of Cape Town, Durban and Johannesburg on Friday calling for an end to the xenophobic violence that is fanned by anti-immigrant groups. Led by Operation Ubuntu and Siyafana Sonke Campaign, and backed by over 80 civil society organisations, the protesters delivered a memorandum of demands to the South African Police Services and various government departments.


The first stop for the Cape Town protest was at the Cape Town Central Police Station where the recently appointed provincial police commissioner, Lt Gen Sizakhele Dyantyi. received the memorandum. The protesters called for an end to the xenophobia perpetrated by the police, and for the arrest and prosecution of March & March ringleaders.


“Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma, Nkosikhona Ndabandaba (Phakel’umthakathi), Ngizwe Mchunu have to be arrested and prosecuted for hate speech, inciting violence, and in Phakel’umthakathi’s case, assaulting migrants. Their actions have led to the forced removal of 160,000 people, our largest forced removal ever. The state has protected them before and since June 30, letting them act with impunity, which has emboldened vigilante groups,” said Shaheed Mohamed, secretary of the Worker International Vanguard League.


Outside parliament in Cape Town, protesters handed over a memorandum of demands to representatives from the departments of Human Settlement, Home Affairs, and Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs (Cogta), as well as the Presidency.


They demanded that the Department of Human Settlement work with social justice and community structures to come up with a fresh bill on land and housing that is informed by community experiences and supported by existing research. In June, land and housing organisations

rejected the Prevention of Illegal Eviction Amendment Bill

and called on the government to deal with the housing crisis instead.


The memorandum stated that Cogta should implement disaster relief in all the areas where migrants are displaced in order to provide humanitarian relief and that there should be negotiation and reintegration as per the South African report on migration of 2023.


From Home Affairs, they demanded that the White Paper on Citizenship and Immigration be halted as some sections are deemed unconstitutional. For instance, the white paper proposes that asylum seekers are not by right entitled to a fair hearing, which is contrary to the Refugee Convention. “Enact an immediate 2-year moratorium on expulsions (voluntary repatriations) in order to allow African migrants to obtain their documents. Resolve the national identity documentation backlog, which has left an estimated 4-million South Africans without IDs, and address the backlog of expired or unprocessed migrant documentation by providing documentation. End mass expulsions and the prevailing climate of fear around documentation, which is functioning like a new dompas,” reads the memorandum.


The protesters called for an end to the xenophobic violence and for the state to be accountable for its actions.


Congolese Civil Society of South Africa (CCSSA) chairperson, Isaiah Mumbilo called for African unity against xenophobia as divisions are in the interest of colonisers and corporations. “Instead of talking about how to protect our natural and mineral resources that we have in the continent, we are prioritising hate of each other in the form of xenophobia,” he said.


The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has faced war and conflict resulting in an estimated 6-million deaths since 1996, a crisis that is driven by the

violent control and exploitation of lucrative rare minerals and natural resources

.


Activist and feminist, Takwana Maema said that migration is a tool that colonialists and capitalists have always used to pull down black bodies, and take control of land and resources. “We need not be taken into making false choices; we need to reject false choices! We need to unite, we need to look at the economic systems and see that these systems continue to perpetuate the fact that Africa continues to stay at the bottom,” she said.


Amadoda Aqotho, a men’s movement based in Khayelitsha, said that they joined the anti-xenophobia protest because the current xenophobic protests and violence scapegoats African migrants and excuses government and those in power. “We joined our African brothers and sisters because we understand that we should not be fighting each other as those in government and in power benefit …

author: Nabil Ferdaoussi
title: A border spectacle
content:
What happened last Thursday in Ceuta was a

border spectacle

 of surprising scale and scope. Tens of thousands of mainly young fellow Moroccans stormed the gates while others braved the water to enter the enclave. All the elements of the spectacle were there: from images of boisterous youngsters jockeying for entry, to a diplomatic slanging match, to border patrols scrambling to push migrants back to Morocco.

It sounds like a geopolitical déjà vu — almost the same border antics: scene, actors, protagonists, and victims staged in May 2021. In fact, what happened in Ceuta is the third episode of the border spectacle: the first staged in May 2021, the second in September 2024, and here we are watching the third — and perhaps not the last — episode, marking a shift in Morocco’s migration diplomacy to a more coercive approach.

There is no conspiracy theory behind the Ceuta border spectacle; there is only a geopolitical buildup to understand Morocco’s coercive migration diplomacy. The latter has shifted migration governance from policies, practices, and discourses to the direct use of its youth and other racialized African migrants in diplomatic sparring.

Here is the buildup: On December 10, 2020, the Trump administration recognized Morocco’s sovereignty over Western Sahara. This historic moment led Morocco to garner further diplomatic recognition, especially from its traditional allies — not least Spain as a former colonizer. In January 2021, a diplomatic logjam between Morocco and Germany started to simmer following the latter’s criticism of Donald Trump’s proclamation to recognize Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara. This diplomatic friction with Germany prompted Morocco to push the European Union.

Meanwhile, the possibility of meeting Morocco’s expectations, whether by the EU or its member states, proved far-fetched. The diplomatic spat between Morocco and Spain reached its nadir when the latter hosted Brahim Ghali, the leader of the Polisario Front, in April 2021 to seek medical treatment. In a tit-for-tat response, Morocco unleashed over 8,000 migrants, including around 3,000 minors. Santiago Abascal, the leader of the anti-migrant far-right Vox party in Spain, denounced the arrivals, stating Morocco was “launching minors like battering rams” against the Spanish borders.

Now, the same scenario is unfolding after Pedro Sánchez visited Algeria to parley with President Abdelmajid Tebboune over natural gas and Western Sahara.

In Europe, the border spectacle sparked a moral panic that feared the invasion of the southern flanks of Europe, raking up right-wing opprobrium over Sánchez’s progressive yet lax migration policies. Far from being an invasion, the border spectacle staged produced anti-migration fodder for far-right politicians.

The border spectacle has resurfaced the centuries-old colonization of Ceuta and Melilla.

The international public that redeems Sánchez as the proponent of the Palestinian cause and progressive migration reforms is bewildered by Ceuta’s tiny geography at the outer fringe of the African continent, wondering how Spain, and for that matter Europe, will be invaded while in Africa. Some historical context is urgent here to disentangle these “only land borders between Africa and EUrope.”

Depending on one’s geopolitical stance, Ceuta and Melilla are at once enclaves and exclaves. From the colonial standpoint of Spain and the European Union, they are seen as exclaves, embodying the external sovereign extension of Spain and, more recently, Europe. In most academic literature, however, the two cities are enclaves standing as the last remnants of European colonization on the African continent. For Moroccans, the two cities are occupied territories, whose recovery remains an unfinished national project of decolonization.

The dispute over Ceuta and Melilla has shaped a long history of sporadic tensions in the relationship between Morocco and Spain. Its historical roots extend back to the Reconquista (c. 718–1492), culminating in the fall of Al-Andalus, and ended with the expulsion of the Moors, between 718 and 1492, from the Iberian Peninsula to North Africa.

Spain extended its sovereignty beyond the Peninsula to vie for external territorial sovereignty in North Africa, seizing Melilla in 1497 and Ceuta — initially conquered by Portugal in 1415 and then ceded to Spain — in 1668. The two towns served as external bulwarks for the clash between the

Ummah

 of Islam and Christendom. Well …

author: Angel Moore
title: Federal minister says conditions on mining, road projects will mitigate damage to environment
content:
Canada’s minister of Environment and Climate Change says the conditions put on two projects approved by the federal government will help alleviate environmental impacts related to fish, birds and the territory.


Julie Dabrusin told media gathered in Halifax on Wednesday for an announcement about money to help municipalities deal with climate change that there were several consultations during the impact assessment phase, including with Indigenous Peoples.


“There are also conditions attached every time that there is a decision through the impact assessment agency and those conditions are specifically to mitigate those impacts, and they are monitored,” she said in response to a question by APTN News about how far the government will go in approving projects that have adverse effects on the environment. “That’s an important part of the equation that also needs to be included. So, with those projects, as with any others, there are conditions that are taken into account when making that balanced assessment.”


The Crawford Nickel Project is likely to destroy or alter approximately 116 hectares of fish habitat, including the watersheds indicated in this map. Graphic: APTN News.


Crawford Nickel Mine


In the past two months, Dabrusin has approved two projects in northern Ontario.


The first was the Crawford Nickel Mine located 42 kilometres north of Timmins. According to the government, it will be the largest mine in Canada when it starts production. The government said it will “produce high-quality, low-carbon nickel essential for batteries and green steel. It will serve as an anchor of Canada’s global leadership in clean industrial materials.”


The mine, the government said, will “attract $5 billion in investment” and create 5,000 jobs for construction of the project and 1,300 for operations.”


In terms of the climate, “the project’s emissions are nearly 90% lower than the global industry average,” the government said.


Canada has signed business contracts with Mattagami, Matachewan, and Flying Post First Nations and Taykwa Tagamou Nation has “partnered with Canada Nickel Company to invest $20 million in the Crawford Nickel Project,” giving the community an 8.4 per cent stake in the project.


On the environmental side, according to the

impact assessment

, the project will have an “adverse” effect on fish, migratory birds and the lands of the First Nations who are signing onto the project.


According to the 38-page impact assessment released by the government, there are a number of conditions attached to the approval of the mine that the company must abide by, including protecting fish from the mine site.


The impact report said approximately 111 species of migratory birds are either confirmed or assumed to be present in the area, according to the assessment.


“Eleven of these are species at risk (including bank swallow, barn swallow, Canada warbler, chimney swift, eastern whip-poor-will, common nighthawk, evening grosbeak, bobolink, olive-sided flycatcher, yellow rail, and eastern meadowlark),” the report states. “Several species of migratory birds, including waterfowl such as geese, have been identified as species of importance to Indigenous communities.”


There are five conditions binding on the company to protect birds that the proponent needs to carrying out the project “in a manner that protects migratory birds and avoids capturing, killing, taking, injuring or harassing migratory birds or destroying, taking or disturbing their eggs, or damaging, destroying, removing or disturbing nests protected.”


In terms of the damage that will be caused to important sites within the project area, the Mattagami First Nation wrote, “Many sites of cultural significance and value will be irreversibly lost from the project, and related knowledge will not be passed down through generations, hindering cultural continuity.”


The government listed six conditions on the company, Canada Nickel, to “develop, prior to construction and in consultation with Indigenous groups, and relevant authorities… an Archeological and Cultural Resources Management Plan,” the approval letter said. “That includes a chance-find protocol for any previously unidentified structures, sites or things of historical, archaeological, paleontological or architectural significance discovered within the Designated Project area.”


All construction is to be stopped if something is discovered.


The Attawapiskat River in Ring of Fire region of northern …

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Community mourns 4-year-old Ivujivik boy as family seeks answers
content:
Ivujivik residents gathered Thursday afternoon to mourn four-year-old Jusi Pudlayat as his family searches for answers about the medical care he received before his death.


Pudlayat’s funeral was scheduled for 1 p.m., his grandmother, Annie Mangiuk, said in the community’s Facebook group.


Mangiuk had raised concerns about her grandson’s condition in posts to the community Facebook group before his death.


In a July 31 post, she said the boy had been suffering persistent stomach pain, had barely eaten for more than a week and that the family had repeatedly sought medical help.


She said nurses had told the family to give him Advil and Tylenol and that he was not properly assessed despite their concerns.


Nunatsiaq News has attempted through several avenues to contact family members but has not received a response.


The Nunavik Police Service confirmed in an email to Nunatsiaq News that officers responded Aug. 1 to a medical assistance call involving an unconscious four-year-old at a residence in Ivujivik.


Emergency medical services personnel were already transporting the child to the Inuulitsivik Health Centre by the time police responded, deputy Chief Shaun Longstreet said. 


According to the Inuulitsivik Health Centre website, Ivujivik has one head nurse and one clinical nurse stationed there. 


In a later post on Aug.9, Mangiuk said Jusi had died and alleged medical staff in Ivujivik and Puvirnituq had not believed the extent of his pain.


Those concerns reached a much wider audience after throat singer Shina Novalinga shared a post about Pudlayat’s death, along with a GoFundMe fundraiser for the family.


Her social media post prompted widespread condolences and renewed discussion about access to health care in Indigenous communities. 


Federal Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty, the Liberal MP for Abitibi—Baie-James—Nunavik—Eeyou, extended condolences Wednesday to Pudlayat’s family through a statement on Facebook.


“It was heartbreaking to hear of the passing of a 4-year-old boy in Ivujivik, in my riding,” Gull-Masty said.


“We expect the Province of Quebec and the medical staff involved to address this matter with the utmost seriousness and to ensure that the system can provide answers to the

family and community while also working to prevent future tragedies from occurring.”


The Inuulitsivik Health Centre and Nunavik Regional Board of Health and Social Services issued a joint statement Wednesday evening, announcing several reviews have been launched into the circumstances surrounding the child’s death.


The health centre’s clinical directorates have begun a multidisciplinary review, while the coroner has initiated an investigation, the statement said.


The coroner’s investigation, which takes place when a death has occurred under violent, unclear or negligent circumstances, takes about six to 12 months, said Quebec Coroner’s Office spokesperson Jake Lamotta Granato in an email.


The health and social services board’s service quality and complaints commissioner is also involved, and an independent medical examiner from outside the Inuulitsivik Health Centre will review the case. 


Québec solidaire, the province’s left-leaning political party, is calling for Quebec’s children’s rights and welfare commissioner to examine Jusi’s death. 


“If this is, once again, a case of systemic racism in our health-care system, it must be clearly identified and action taken accordingly,” party spokesperson Sol Zanetti said in a French statement Thursday.

author: Mehran Khalili
title: It’s time for movements to rethink social media
content:
This article

It’s time for movements to rethink social media

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


Last September I made

a short video

 that was by far the most viral piece of content I’ve ever put out.


I can’t trace all the views, but at least a million people watched it across Instagram and TikTok, and possibly elsewhere. Neighbors in Athens, Greece told me they’d come across my face in their feed; Chinese accounts captioned the video and reposted it. I felt like I’d made a dent in the universe and — I’m not going to lie — a little bit special.


The video wasn’t pop wisdom or a dance routine. It had a job to do: get people to sign a

petition

, created by DiEM25 and Progressive International, to block Germany’s genocide-enabling former foreign minister, Annalena Baerbock, from becoming president of the U.N. General Assembly. 


And on that, it failed. By the end of my week of internet mini-fame, the number of signatures had barely shifted. It had 49,000 signatures that July, two months before I posted. I watched it closely that week, and it barely moved.  Baerbock got the job – the petition now

asks her to resign

. 


I know a few things about digital communication. For two decades it’s been a key part of what I do — I’ve written about it, researched it, advised movements on it. The petition wasn’t mine, but the video was. And I couldn’t make it work. 


Maybe the video could have been packaged better, or the petition link made easier to find. Maybe my pitch was entertaining but not compelling. Maybe a petition was never the right vehicle for stopping Baerbock in the first place.


My organizer friends thought it went great. They congratulated me on the numbers. Nobody asked about the petition.


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


That last part is what’s bothered me since. Because if a million views and no signatures is considered a success, we’re measuring the wrong thing.


And that opens up a bigger question, one I don’t think we ask often enough: When we use social media in our organizing, what are we actually doing? Is it worth the time we put into it? And is there a way of doing it that actually builds something?


Why we’re all on there anyway


Social media is now a given for organizers, and for good reason. We’ve been using it to fill public squares for well over a decade, from Occupy to Black Lives Matter to last year’s

Gen Z protests

 across the Global South. To get around media blackouts and show the world what power does when it thinks no one’s filming, from Ferguson to Gaza. To

make

 and

sink

 political careers. To

tank the stock prices

 of corporations that deserve it. 


Social media has changed how we communicate. It’s forced us to be quicker, sharper and more entertaining. Because attention is scarce — and we’re competing for it against everything else.


But beneath all of this, most of us are working from the same assumption: that

platforms are where the work happens

. That the posting is the organizing. That if we get the reach, the rest will follow.


What changed


That assumption has a history. Those of us who were around in 2011 will remember that social media held a different kind of promise. We thought we could topple governments and kings, if only we could get enough people onto the streets. And social media was very good at getting people onto the streets, as long as the anger was already there.


Sometimes that was enough. Tunisian dictator

Ben Ali

 went. Egyptian dictator

Mubarak

 went. But when it didn’t hold — when Occupy dissolved, when Tahrir Square gave way to

a military government

, when the squares emptied — we told ourselves it wasn’t the right moment, or that the repression was too heavy.


My sense is that a lot of us still carry that same idealism about social media’s power. But two things have changed since then.


The first is that governments got very good at pushing us back. They stifle protest at the source now, with monitoring, arrests and social media operations of their own. Movements can still get around censorship, and often do. But the state has learned to work on the same terrain. Amnesty International has documented how last year Kenyan authorities

used the same platforms

 as the Gen Z movement to threaten and discredit organizers.  And where that isn’t enough, the state can reach for the platform itself — banning it, as

Nepal did in 2025

, or changing who owns …

author: Frey Blake-Pijogge, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: ‘Foundational instability’: As permafrost thaws, Nunainguk’s ground is shifting beneath its residents’ feet
content:
Chaim Andersen, infrastructure planning co-ordinator for the Nunatsiavut Government.

Photo by Frey Blake-Pijogge


This story was originally published in 

The Narwhal

 and appears here with minor style edits. 


In central Nunainguk (Nain), the largest community in

Nunatsiavut

 (northern “Labrador”), Joey Angnatok used shipping containers to build his warehouse.


He placed the two sea cans on hefty steel H-beams, leaving some room beneath them, should he need to jack up one end or the other against the sloping, ever-changing ground.


The land under them, he says, is “alive, like it’s always moving.” 


Some of the Nunatsiavut region is underlaid with permafrost, a layer of soil, sediment, rock and ice — sometimes all of them together — that remains frozen for more than two years.


Permafrost is ubiquitous across the Arctic and much of the subarctic. Some of the oldest layers are believed to have remained frozen for hundreds of thousands of years.


But despite its longevity in some places, as the climate warms, permafrost thaw is becoming an increasingly inescapable problem.


“I hate it,” Angnatok says, “because I own a few properties around town, and unfortunately the melting of the permafrost is playing havoc with the foundations and movements of the buildings.” 


READ MORE:


Climate change is melting ice roads — a lifeline for remote Indigenous communities


That’s why he built his warehouse to mitigate the undulating effects of permafrost thaw.


“Because the land was so bad there,” he explains, “I figured we’d try something different instead of your normal ‘pour the concrete down and then build your wood structure on that.’” 


Three years after building, he says he’s still holding his breath. 


Nunainguk, the administrative capital of Nunatsiavut, is a community at the forefront of change.


What’s happening here is being seen elsewhere in the

North

, and is predicted to continue as the climate warms — thawing and reshaping the foundations on which communities are built.


As “Canada” eyes expansion and development in the Arctic, thawing permafrost could have a big impact.


Lichens, crowberry and bakeapple thrive on permafrost, offering animals vital food sources — and impacting wildlife as it thaws


A peat plateau near ‘Rigolet, Labrador.’ The slightly raised permafrost is surrounded by wetter peatland.

Photos courtesy Yifeng Wang


Climate change and human activity drive permafrost thaw


In another part of the community, there used to be a convenience store, Puffin Snacks, in which everything — including the building itself — was tilted to one side.


“If you walked into the building, you just started running in,” recalls local resident Michelle Saunders, research manager with the Nunatsiavut Government, “because it was just so sloped.” 


Puffin Snacks, too, was built on permafrost.


A study on 

permafrost in the town

, published in 2021, shows that much of the infrastructure across the community has been impacted in some way as the ground shifts and sinks beneath it.


As the climate changes — far faster in the Arctic than elsewhere around the world — permafrost is thawing as temperatures rise. 


Robert Way, an associate professor at Queen’s University in the Department of Geography and Planning, is from “Labrador” and is one of the authors of the study on permafrost in the town.


READ MORE:


IndigiNews reporting from the North


Spending three to four months each year in “Happy Valley-Goose Bay, Labrador,” he studies the impacts of climate change in the subarctic region. 


In addition to climate change, Way says human activities such as construction of buildings and roads can also impact permafrost.


“Building a house over top of permafrost, especially in areas where the permafrost is relatively warmer, often will contribute more heat into the system,” he explains, “and will result in permafrost starting to thaw.”


Additionally, building roads leads to stripping vegetation and piling up snow, which he says can also impact the permafrost underneath. 


These changes are on the minds of Saunders and her colleagues, as they manage and facilitate research programs in and with Nunatsiavut communities.


It affects their personal lives too.


Michelle Saunders, a Nunainguk resident and research manager for the Nunatsiavut Government, worries about building a cabin on shifting ground.

Photo by Frey Blake-Pijogge


Saunders, who moved to Nunainguk five years ago, is thinking of …

author: C4SS
title: Insureksi atau Revolusi?
content:
Saul Newman

. Teks aslinya berjudul “

Insurrection

 or Revolution?

”. Diterjemahkan ke dalam Bahasa Indonesia oleh Taratsa.


Pada saat narasi besar tentang Revolusi yang kita warisi dari modernitas dan diskursus rasionalis Pencerahan hampir runtuh, apa alternatif yang ada untuk mengonseptualisasikan transformasi radikal? Meski tidak adanya kelas atau gerakan revolusioner yang terorganisir, pada saat yang sama kaum kiri tidak mampu berpikir melampaui gagasan emansipasi revolusioner. Kegagalan imajinasi radikal inilah yang mungkin menjadi alasan kebuntuan politik yang dihadapi kaum kiri saat ini.


Karena tidak mampu menciptakan perubahan yang bermakna, kaum kiri malah terjebak dalam “perang budaya” dan terlibat dalam politik identitas melawan kaum kanan yang jauh lebih terampil memainkan permainan ini. Dogmatisme puritan dan semangat keagamaan yang mengiringi perdebatan tanpa akhir tentang identitas gender, ras, inklusi kaum marginal, dan sebagainya menunjukkan kelelahan tertentu dari horizon politik radikal.


Menjadikan politik didasarkan pada pengakuan identitas, di satu sisi, dan janji masa depan tentang keselamatan revolusioner, di sisi lain, berarti jatuh ke dalam perangkap kekuasaan negara. Negara difetiskan baik sebagai entitas yang memberikan hak dan status hukum kepada minoritas, maupun sebagai musuh yang harus ditaklukkan agar kebebasan dapat diwujudkan—ilusi yang, sebagaimana ditunjukkan oleh sejarah revolusi, hanya menghasilkan negara-negara baru dan bentuk-bentuk despotisme baru.


Mungkin sudah waktunya untuk meninggalkan “bayangan (spooks)” identitas dan revolusi, serta memikirkan subyektivitas dan politik dengan cara yang berbeda. Di sinilah saya mengusulkan untuk kembali pada filsuf anarkis egois abad ke-19, Max Stirner. Dalam karya

The Ego and Its Own

 (

Der Einzige und sein Eigentum

), yang diterbitkan pada tahun 1844, Stirner mengusulkan bentuk aksi politik alternatif yang ia sebut “Insureksi” (

Insurrection

 atau

Empörung

), yang ia bandingkan dengan Revolusi.


Jika Revolusi adalah proyek yang bertujuan mengubah hubungan sosial dan politik eksternal, maka insureksi adalah transformasi diri. Ini adalah cara bagi individu untuk mengatasi kepatuhan sukarela dan identifikasinya dengan otoritas. Dengan demikian, insureksi tidak menutup kemungkinan terjadinya perubahan sosial dan politik yang lebih luas, tetapi perubahan tersebut didasarkan pada tindakan awal pembebasan diri ini—perubahan dalam cara kita berhubungan dengan diri sendiri dan orang lain.


Sebagaimana dikatakan Stirner, insureksi memiliki konsekuensi tak terhindarkan berupa transformasi keadaan, “namun tidak dimulai dari keadaan tersebut, melainkan dari ketidakpuasan manusia terhadap dirinya sendiri.” Dengan demikian, insureksi dapat dilihat sebagai bentuk emansipasi diri yang radikal. Insureksi tidak dipandu atau ditentukan oleh pelopor revolusioner atau partai-partai, dan ia tidak berusaha merebut serta mengendalikan kekuasaan negara.


Sebaliknya, ia secara radikal anti-institusional: “Revolusi bertujuan pada pengaturan baru; insureksi membawa kita untuk tidak lagi diatur, tetapi mengatur diri kita sendiri, dan tidak menggantungkan harapan pada ‘institusi’.” Negara tidak dilihat sebagai instrumen transformasi sosial, atau bahkan sebagai hambatan utama kebebasan individu. Insureksi menolak fetisisasi kekuasaan negara ini. Individu egois harus menegaskan dirinya di atas negara; ia tidak lagi melihat negara, baik dalam kekaguman maupun ketakutan (dua sisi mata uang yang sama), melainkan hanya pada dirinya sendiri.


Gagasan unik tentang insureksi ini adalah bagian kunci dari proyek filosofis dan etis egoisme Stirner. Bagi Stirner, di dunia yang penuh dengan “bayangan (spooks)” atau abstraksi ideologis dan ideal-ideal metafisik—seperti kemanusiaan, moralitas, kebebasan, hak, masyarakat, hukum, dan negara—yang merupakan sisa-sisa dari agama namun terus menghantui kita, ego adalah satu-satunya realitas konkret, satu-satunya hal yang nyata dan dapat disentuh.


Namun, apa sebenarnya yang dimaksud Stirner dengan ego? Kesalahan umum adalah ketika menyamakannya dengan “individu,” seperti yang sering dilakukan dalam diskursus liberal dan libertarian. Ego jauh lebih cair dan menghindari semua kategorisasi semacam itu atau gagasan “tetap” lainnya. Faktanya, kita dapat mengatakan bahwa ego adalah semacam non-identitas radikal yang tidak dapat dikaitkan dengan bentuk subjektivitas apa pun atau ditentukan oleh karakteristik esensial apa …

author: Valerie Anne
title: Ted Lasso Is Back and Promises To Be Gayer Than Ever
content:
Over three years since the season three finale, Ted Lasso is back! In the fourth season premiere, his old colleagues Rebecca (Hannah Waddingham), bisexual baddie Keeley (Juno Temple), and Higgins (Jeremy Swift) come to him with a job offer: coaching their new women’s football team. And as we well know, with women’s soccer comes lesbians, and though we don’t know all the details yet, we know at the very least there will be a lot more queer representation in the coming season than there was in the past few.

What we do know comes mostly from Coach Jackie on TikTok, who was on the red carpet asking the important question to the actors of this season: “Are you playing a lesbian?” Some people were coy about it, but at least two actors already admitted their characters are lesbians, and one actor said she is sadly not playing a lesbian BUT introduced Coach Jackie to her wife, who says she looks like Sue Bird. Also in the cast is nonbinary actor Faye Marsay and Tanya Reynolds, who has played queer before in Sex Education.

Two things people learn quickly upon getting to know me is that men and sports are two of the things I care least about in the world. So it surprised myself as much as anyone else how much I loved the first three seasons of this show. Ted Lasso and his boys kicked their way into my heart one ripped up piece of a BELIEVE sign at a time. I love that it tackled topics like toxic masculinity and homophobia with a lot of honesty and heart. That said, I am REALLY looking forward to a women-dominated season, where I have no doubt they’ll cover topics like sexism and the disparity between men and women’s sports, tucked into its natural charm and humor.

Bonus: It seems the new cast enjoyed their time on set. Tanya Reynolds said, “It’s been a joy to go to work every day, because everyone is so nice.” Adding in my favorite lore drop: “There are no dickheads.”

The first episode of Ted Lasso is available on Apple TV now, with new episodes dropping every Wednesday.

+ Nonbinary star of gay reality show I Kissed a Girl, Pippa Palmer, has started a new LGBTQ+ app called Queer Connected that will help people find local events and groups and such, inspired by their own difficulty making queer friends when they were coming out

+ Lucy Dacus performed Bullseye with Julien Baker at the Outside Lands festival this weekend, calling her out by saying she wanted to bring her “best friend” to the stage

+ House of the Dragon has aired its season three finale and seems to be a turning point for Emma D’Arcy’s Queen Rhaenyra

+ Whitney Houston is getting her own Barbie, dressed in her classic “I Wanna Dance With Somebody” outfit

+ Bicon Aubrey Plaza had her baby!

+ For its 60th anniversary, actors in the franchise look back on Star Trek‘s queer characters and actors that have appeared on its various shows throughout the years

+ Ariana Grande’s album, Petal, reached #1 on the Billboard music charts

author: Elizabeth Weill-Greenberg
title: After More Than 20 Years in Prison, Georgia Man Wins New Trial in “Shaken Baby” Case
content:
A Georgia court has

ordered a new trial

 for Danyel Smith, a father who was convicted of killing his two-month-old son, Chandler, more than twenty years ago. Prosecutors relied on a diagnosis of Shaken Baby Syndrome (SBS) to secure his conviction. In recent years, scientific evidence has emerged calling into question the basic assumptions behind the hypothesis.


In her decision, Gwinnett County Superior Court Judge Kimberly A. Gallant ruled that the evolving research into SBS, also known as Abusive Head Trauma (AHT), constitutes new evidence that was not known at the time of trial. 


“Mr. Smith’s evidence is not based on historical facts or eyewitness testimony, but on expert analysis grounded in the application of evolving scientific knowledge,” Gallant wrote in

her decision

. 


Medical experts for the defense

have concluded

 that Chandler was not the victim of abuse.


The defense experts surmise that on the day he fell unconscious, he had a seizure, went into respiratory distress, and stopped breathing. This was at least the second seizure Chandler, who was born five-weeks premature, had experienced, according to Smith’s legal filings. When he was less than two weeks old his mother called 911 and reported that he was breathing strangely and appeared to be having a seizure. The responding paramedics dismissed her concerns. (Smith was not home at the time.)


The expert opinions underlying his motion for a new trial, the judge wrote, “are informed by research advancements in medicine, scientific developments, peer-reviewed literature, and evolving medical standards.”


At the time of Smith’s trial, there was largely a consensus among the scientific and legal communities about the veracity of SBS/AHT. But in the decades since, exonerations and studies have revealed that the so-called

triad of symptoms

 associated with SBS/AHT—bleeding around the eyes, bleeding between the skull and brain, and brain swelling—can be caused by strokes, short-distance falls, childbirth trauma, and disease. 


What was once considered to be virtually unassailable evidence of abuse is now,

in the words of one New Jersey judge

, increasingly understood to be “akin to ‘junk science.’”


The Appeal in Your Inbox


Subscribe to our newsletters for regular updates, analysis and context straight to your email.


Sign Up


On April 29, 2002, Smith was driving his eight-week-old son, Chandler, to a benefits office so that his partner could apply for food assistance. On the ride over, Smith looked at Chandler when he was stopped at a red light and saw that he was pale and not breathing, according to Smith’s motion for a new trial. Smith’s petition says that in a “frantic phone call” he told his partner that something was wrong with the baby and drove to where she was waiting. 


He carried the baby out of the car and Chandler’s mother called 911. Bystanders attempted to perform CPR. When the paramedics arrived, they took Chandler to the hospital.  


The next day, a child abuse specialist examined Chandler and concluded that he had been shaken. On May 1, Smith was arrested at the hospital. Less than a week later, his son was taken off life support and died.


“[T]here’s no other explanation that the doctors might look for that would explain these symptoms, other than non-accidental trauma, that is, child abuse,” the prosecutor told the jury during opening arguments at Smith’s trial. 


The county medical examiner testified that Chandler’s injuries “are classic and in some cases virtually exclusive for violent shaking.”


Smith maintained his innocence.


“I did not shake my son,” Smith told the jury.


On November 21, 2003, Smith was convicted of felony murder, cruelty to children, and aggravated battery. The judge sentenced him to life in prison.


Smith has never stopped trying to prove his innocence. In 2021, the Southern Center for Human Rights took up his case and began an exhaustive investigation.


In 2021, Smith’s attorneys filed a petition for a new trial, but did not receive an evidentiary hearing until 2024. Prior to the hearing, the Gwinnett County prosecutor’s office

offered Smith a plea deal

. In exchange for pleading guilty, he would get time served and be released from prison, according to Smith’s legal filings. Smith rejected it. 


“He’s now served 24 years in prison, that’s half of his life,” Smith’s attorney, Mark Loudon-Brown, told The Appeal. “During that time, he turned down the opportunity to go home simply …

author: Admin101
title: The Platform at 100: Voices of Organized Anarchists Around the Globe (Vol. 2)
content:
To mark the 100 year anniversary of the publication of the

Platform of Libertarian Communists (Draft)

, we are excited to present the second in a three volume series of interviews discussing the document’s lasting legacy with anarchist organizations around the world

.


The Platform, as it is often called by shorthand, was written by a group of Russian and Ukranian anarchists exiled in the wake of the Bolshevik seizure of state power during the 1917 October Revolution. The document was meant to be a corrective to the prevailing anarchist orthodoxy of the time, which its authors—including

Nestor Makhno

 and other active participants in the revolution—believed had led to their defeat.


Note:

 Originally we had planned to release all of the interviews in two volumes. However, the number of organizations who requested to participate


and the length of the content requires us to break the interviews up into three volumes.


The

first volume

 covered organizations in the Americas,

this second volume covers organizations in Europe

, and the third will cover organizations in Asia and Oceania.


This project is a collaboration between the External Education and International Relations Committees of Black Rose/Rosa Negra (BRRN).


Table of Contents

Introduction

Union Communiste Libertaire (France)

Die Plattform (Germany)

Anarchist Communist Group (UK)

Midada (Switzerland)

Liza (Spain)

Embat (Catalonia)


Download


the Pamphlet

Version


Introduction


2026 marks 100 years since the publication of the

Organizational Platform of the Libertarian Communists (Draft)

 by the Dielo Truda (Workers’ Cause) group. The document, written by Russian, Belarusian, and Ukrainian anarchists exiled in the wake of the 1917 October Revolution in Russia, is known for the sharp revisions it applied to the contemporary anarchist orthodoxy. Though criticized by some of the most prominent anarchist thinkers of the period,

the Platform

 (as it has come to be known by shorthand) represents a first serious attempt to grapple with organizational and strategic shortcomings in the anarchist movement, exposed by its direct involvement in a large-scale revolutionary upheaval.


While it is true that the Dielo Truda group set a course distinct from many of their anarchist contemporaries, the novelty of the principles put forward in the Platform is often overstated. The central concern of the Platform’s authors was a more effective coordination of anarchist militants aiming to intervene in social movements. The Dielo Truda group arrived at the conclusion that this could only be achieved through the construction of a revolutionary political organization. Indeed, this same insight was achieved by Mikhail Bakunin more than half a century earlier as he helped to found the Alliance of Socialist Democracy, which was later dissolved into the International Workingmen’s Association (also known as the First International). In other words, far from being a recent invention, the anarchist embrace of formal revolutionary political organization can be traced back to the movement’s origins.


Today we recognize this insight as ‘organizational dualism,’ a phrase that refers to the necessity of, and reciprocal relationship between, revolutionary political organization and mass organization. While organizations interviewed in this survey may identify to a greater or lesser extent with a particular historical framework—most commonly platformism or especifismo—all hold the organizational dualist principle as a central tenet.


Union Communiste Libertaire

 (France)


1.


UCL was formed in 2019 as a fusion of two existing organizations,

Coordination des Groupes Anarchistes (CGA)

 and Alternative Libertaire (AL). Can you briefly explain what brought these two groups together and what the process of becoming one organization involved?


UCL:

AL and CGA were two relatively small organisations. They didn’t have the exact same background but they shared theoretical references and a similar intervention into the global struggle of the people. 


The growth of both organizations was slowing. Both organizations got used to working together, and the election of Emmanuel Macron meant a strengthening of attacks against the working class. For our political tradition, the organization isn’t the be-all and end-all of our political activity but a tool in the service of our movement. It felt natural to attempt a fusion.

title: This Day in Anarchist History – The Establishment of the Korean Anarchist Federation in Manchuria
content: ﻿ Born out of the Korean diaspora in Manchuria escaping brutal Japanese colonial rule and in the power vacuum left in the wake of the assassination of the local warlord, the Korean Anarchist Federation existed against all odds. The Korean Anarchist Federation would go on to merge with the Now People’s Government to form the Korean People’s Association in Manchuria which at it’s peak organized 2 million people according to the anarchist principals of collective farming, arms training, free education and mutual aid.
