title: High school, university students walk out of class to protest Hanson’s bigotry
content:
High school, university students walk out of class to protest Hanson’s bigotry


Isaac Nellist


Thu, 13/08/2026 - 19:08


Isaac Nellist


August 13, 2026

,


Issue 1460

,


News


Thousands of students joined protests across the country opposing the racism and bigotry of Pauline Hanson and One Nation on August 13. 


See also


Reject One Nation’s call to return to White Australia Policy


How fossil fuel companies target children with climate disinformation


Domestic violence isn’t a ‘two-way street’ and Hanson isn’t confused


The protests were called by the National Union of Students and buoyed by a big turn out of high school students, who skipped school classes to attend the rally. 


The impressive turnout, particularly of high school students, reflects the anger among many young people that Hanson’s far-right politics are getting a hearing in the corporate media, and in-turn being reflected in high polling figures across the country. 


While One Nation has been consistently polling between 25-30%, its support among “Gen Z”, 14–29-year-olds, is around 10%. 


Thousands of students joined the protest in Gadigal Country/Sydney. Photo: Zebedee Parkes


The rally in Gadigal Country/Sydney was electric, with big groups of students arriving with homemade placards, often still wearing their school uniforms. 


University students rallied on campuses across the city before converging on Sydney Town Hall. Students from the University of Sydney briefly took over Redfern Station with chants of “Whose station? Our station!” before catching the train across to Town Hall. 


While many students travelled from nearby inner-city high schools, others travelled from as far as the Blue Mountains, Central Coast and even regional New South Wales to join the rally. 


Students were eager to show their opposition to Hanson's racism. Photo: Peter Boyle


About 2000 students and supporters filled the Town Hall Square, where they heard speeches from student activists and NSW Greens MP Jenny Leong.


References to Hanson, Barnaby Joyce and billionaire Gina Rinehart were met with boos, while calls against racism, transphobia and misogyny were loudly cheered. One student commented that it “felt like a music festival” because of the outpouring of energy and enthusiasm from the youth. 


While anti-racism and opposition to Hanson’s “monoculture” was a key theme, many young people also held signs supporting LGBTIQ rights. 


Protesters then marched around the block before returning to Town Hall Square for a final rally.


A high school student addresses the Gadigal Country/Sydney rally. Photo: Zebedee Parkes


Some of the students who joined the Boorloo/Perth protest. Photo: Petrina Harley

author: Carissa Lee
title: MEDIA STATEMENT : FELIPE ALVAREZ CORONIAL INQUEST
content:
FELIPE ALVAREZ: FAMILY CALLS FOR ACCOUNTABILITY, TRANSPARENCY AND CORONIAL REFORM AFTER ACT CORONER’S FINDINGS


By Gabriela Alvarez-Sledge

Sister of the late Felipe Esteban Alvarez


Disclaimer: Readers please be advised this article mentions someone who has passed away.


“Felipe’s life mattered. His death mattered. What we learn from his death matters.”


The family of the late

Felipe Esteban Alvarez

 is calling for greater transparency, accountability and reform of the ACT coronial system following the release of the findings into his death.


Felipe died in March 2021 following an overdose at his Canberra residence.


Five years later, his family is still grieving while asking an important question:


What can be changed so that another family does not have to go through what ours has experienced?


Felipe was not simply a coronial file.


He was a brother, son, uncle and deeply loved member of his family.


His life had value.


His family believes his death deserved to be investigated as thoroughly, transparently and independently as possible.


WHAT THE CORONER FOUND


The findings of ACT Coroner Ken Archer identified serious concerns surrounding the circumstances of Felipe’s death.


The Coroner found that Felipe was experiencing a medical emergency and that emergency medical assistance was not sought for a significant period of time.


The Coroner found that the delay deprived Felipe of any chance of survival he may have had following his initial collapse.


The Coroner described the conduct of those present as

“morally blameworthy”

 and found that their conduct demonstrated a serious indifference to the possibility of loss of life.


The findings also identified broader public-safety concerns relating to the Canberra Alliance for Harm Minimisation and Advocacy (CAHMA), including concerns about governance, recruitment and screening, overdose-response training, naloxone availability and organisational accountability.


The Coroner found that appropriate screening and eligibility processes should have been applied to the relevant peer workers.


The findings also raised concerns about the organisation’s response following Felipe’s death and the need for stronger governance and accountability.


The Coroner recommended improvements to overdose-response training and stronger collaboration between harm-minimisation services, health agencies, ambulance services and police.


The family welcomes those recommendations.


THE FAMILY’S CONCERNS REMAIN


Throughout the coronial process, Felipe’s family provided information, documents and concerns about matters they believed were important to understanding what happened.


The family identified people who were present when Felipe suffered his overdose and sought to have the relevant evidence properly considered.


The family also provided written material that it believed was relevant to understanding what occurred.


However, the family remained concerned that not every matter it believed was important was fully tested or explored during the coronial process.


Because the Court has imposed restrictions concerning the publication of identities,

the family will not identify any person whose identity is subject to suppression

.


The family respects the Court’s orders.


There will be no naming of suppressed individuals in this statement.


The family’s concern has never been about publicly naming people.


It is about evidence.


It is about transparency.


It is about whether families can have confidence that every reasonable avenue of inquiry has been considered when their loved one dies.


THIS IS NOT AN ATTACK ON THE CORONER


The family wishes to make this position very clear.


Gabriela   Alvarez-Sledge is not seeking to undermine the independence of the Coroner or interfere with the findings.


She acknowledges the Coroner’s findings and welcomes the public-safety recommendations.


The family’s concern is about what can be learned from the entire experience.


A coronial system should not only determine how a person died.


It should also give bereaved families confidence that the investigation was thorough, transparent, fair and independent.


Where families continue to have genuine concerns about aspects of a coronial process, there should be an appropriate and independent pathway for those concerns to be considered.


A CALL FOR CORONIAL REFORM

author: AWSM
title: A Community in the Cracks of Capitalism
content:
A piece of Christchurch that the property market abandoned after the earthquakes has become home to people abandoned by the property market. The old Bexley neighbourhood was largely cleared after liquefaction made conventional residential development impossible. Houses disappeared, streets remained and the land sat waiting for whatever official purpose would eventually be found for it. Into that gap came people who needed somewhere to live. They arrived in cars, vans, buses and tents. Some were working. Some were retired. Some had children. They did what people have always done when the institutions around them fail, they improvised. A community grew. Earlier this year about 40 people were living around Wetlands Grove; reports now put the number at more than 100. Christchurch City Council has told them they must leave by 28 February 2027 because the area is intended for wetland development. There is an obvious temptation to treat this as a story about homelessness, council planning or the difficulties of finding somewhere suitable for a group of people living in vehicles. It is all of those things, but underneath them sits a much simpler question. What is land for? The answer given by our economic system is that land belongs to whoever has legal title to it, and its legitimate use is determined by owners, planners and institutions. The people actually living on it remain secondary. They may sleep there, look after one another there and make the place usable through their own effort, but none of that gives them any meaningful claim to it. Their relationship to the place exists only for as long as the legal owner tolerates it. That distinction between ownership and use lies close to the heart of the anarchist criticism of private property.

The people living at Wetlands Grove have already demonstrated something that governments spend enormous amounts of money trying unsuccessfully to manufacture through policy documents – people can organise social life themselves. Earlier reporting described an informal community growing around buses, vans and cars, with neighbours helping one another through winter and a communal tent being established as shared space. One man who had been sleeping in a small tent was helped into an old car when the cold became severe. Council rubbish collection and portable toilets made conditions more bearable, but the social organisation of the place came largely from the people living there. Moko, one of the informal figures in the community, was working full-time on an on-call road crew. Others were pensioners. Ngawai Timu described abandoning a $470-a-week rental because she felt she was spending her life paying somebody else’s mortgage. Polly Stewart was surviving on the pension in a bus. Families were living there too, including a woman with several children living from a bus. These details matter because homelessness is constantly spoken about as though it were primarily a pathology of homeless people. Addiction, mental illness, poor budgeting, antisocial behaviour and bad choices are summoned as explanations because those explanations leave the social order intact. They allow us to imagine that housed people possess some quality that homeless people lack. Wetlands Grove makes that story harder to sustain. When people with jobs cannot obtain housing, when pensioners decide rent leaves too little for ordinary life, and when families find themselves competing with dozens of others for a private rental, the problem is no longer plausibly located inside the individual. There are certainly people living rough who struggle with addiction or serious psychological distress. There are also people who get up and go to work from a tent. A housing system that cannot reliably house either has failed at the most elementary level.

New Zealand has become remarkably skilled at describing this failure without challenging the institution producing it. We talk about housing supply, affordability pressures and housing need. We devise eligibility categories and waiting lists. We construct administrative pathways through emergency housing, transitional housing, community housing and social housing. Every stage acquires its own assessments and rules. The language becomes more sophisticated while people remain without homes. At the 2023 Census, Statistics New Zealand estimated that at least 112,496 people were experiencing severe housing deprivation, around 2.3 percent of the usually resident population. The …

author: Luca Tavan
title: Rebel teachers taking their campaign against the Labor government all the way to parliament
content:
“I’m a rebel teacher running against Ben Carroll in Niddrie because I think workers should run the world. I think teachers know how to run schools, and we should be empowered to run the education system ... On the issue of education, the ALP is not just out of touch: they’re on the other side of the picket line, with the Liberals and One Nation.”

This is how Brendan Laws announced the Victorian “rebel educator” campaign—a group of teachers and education support staff targeting sitting Labor MPs, including Premier and former Minister for Education Ben Carroll. 

The eight candidates, all members of Victorian Socialists and the Socialists in Schools union group, have played a role in leading the rank-and-file rebellion in the Australian Education Union (AEU) Victorian Branch that has organised two massive strike days, stared down the state government and fought tooth and nail against the conservative leadership of their own union. The teachers’ fight is the most significant industrial dispute in Victoria in years, with teachers holding the line for a decent contract in the context of falling real wages and deteriorating working conditions. For many on the left, the obstinacy of Victorian Labor in the face of teachers’ demands for decent pay and tolerable working conditions embodies everything wrong with a government which once boasted of running “the most progressive state in the nation”.

Labor has governed Victoria practically uninterrupted for more than two decades, leaning heavily on the support of union members to win successive elections. AEU members were a central part of the mobilisation of 2,200 unionists who doorknocked and phone-banked to hand Daniel Andrews a surprise victory in 2014. 

Twelve years on, Victoria has the lowest-funded public schools in the country. The government has stolen $16 billion from the system through underfunding in the last seven years alone. Surging workloads, wage suppression and increasing class sizes have created a situation in which less than a third of teachers plan to stay in the sector long-term. 

Leading teacher unionist and Victorian Socialists candidate for Niddrie Brendan Laws says:

“The school I’m working at right now is relatively well resourced, but the sheer amount of work and stress is overwhelming. You’re writing and rewriting assessments, you’re marking, trying to give individual feedback. There’s this pressure, because the school is competing with over-funded private schools ... I was at a very low-income school in Werribee; you could see all the traps that students get pulled into, not having the resources to read and learn, at the same time as [Labor] were spending hundreds of millions of dollars on a nearby youth prison. You would just see the kids that were getting pulled out of school into that constantly. Eight teachers quit from my department during one school year so there weren’t enough staff and everybody else had to pull in just to fill in the gaps.”

The AEU leadership’s close-knit relationship with the Labor government means many educators feel the officials have worked against members’ interests. Workers went backwards after their 2022 contract negotiation, when the AEU leadership rushed through a sell-out deal cutting real wages by 11 percent. Forty percent of AEU members voted against the offer, at the time a historically unprecedented rejection of a leadership decision in the union. While many left the union in disgust, others waited, and pledged that next time around it would be different  

Brendan was one of around a dozen Victorian Socialists members who decided to launch Socialists in Schools in mid-2025. “The biggest indicator that there was an audience for it was how many AEU members were already part of Victorian Socialists”, he says. “We took a survey and found we had almost 100 teacher members, so it just showed that there was already a base to work with.” 

The campaign started with the modest aim of giving socialist teachers a chance to get together and chat:

“The first part was just meeting up and discussing socialist politics with the people in our campaign. It was the political arguments around militarism, the genocide in Palestine, the Labor government’s austerity and privatisation. Then when we knew that our last agreement was going to expire and the opportunity to have industrial action was going to be there, we really shifted a lot of our propaganda to educate people about striking. It had been 13 years since a strike had …

author: Sheree Lowe
title: Our Children are the Treaty generation
content:
This

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children’s Day

, we have an opportunity to reflect on something remarkable. 


Across Victoria, our Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children are growing up in one of the most significant political moments since colonisation. They are the first generation of children to grow up in

Victoria’s Treaty era

. Treaty is about far more than legal agreements or institutional reform. At its heart, Treaty is about people, and most importantly, our children, and our future generations. 


The true measure of any Treaty will not be found in the number of agreements reached or milestones achieved. It will be measured by whether it truly improves the lives of future generations. 


Will Aboriginal children grow up healthier? Will their identity and Connection to their Culture be strong? Will they have every opportunity to learn, thrive and lead? Will they inherit systems that recognise their strengths rather than focus on their disadvantage? 


These are the questions that really matter. 


Aboriginal children already possess extraordinary strengths. They inherit the oldest continuing culture on Earth. They are surrounded by families, Elders and Communities who pass on knowledge, stories and traditions – keeping them strong and keeping them connected to who they are. 


But despite their strengths, many Aboriginal children continue to experience inequitable outcomes across

health

, education,

incarceration

, and wellbeing. Too often, systems have been designed to exclude Aboriginal people and their families, rather than include them.  


Treaty is our chance to change this.  


Treaty allows us to shift decision-making closer to Aboriginal communities, strengthening self-determination and creating services that better reflect the aspirations, cultures and needs of Aboriginal children and families. 


This is not simply about changing policies. It is about changing possibilities. 


Imagine growing up as an Aboriginal child.

Imagine instead of growing up in a State that perpetuates stigma, stereotypes and wants to dismiss your culture in dark history books – you grow up knowing who you are, where you belong and actually understanding your Country and Culture.  


Children have the potential to grow up in a state where their Culture is not only respected but embedded throughout education, healthcare and public life.  Our collective history recognised, our languages celebrated and Community empowered to shape the services that support our families. 


Imagine knowing that decisions about your future are increasingly made by your own people, your Community.

That is the promise that Treaty represents. 


For today’s Aboriginal children, this is not some distant vision. It is unfolding right now, during their own childhood. 


They are the first generation who will remember Victoria before Treaty, and who will one day tell their own children what it was like to witness this historic transformation. 


That is both exciting and humbling, but it also places an extraordinary responsibility on all of us. 


Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children’s Day reminds us that children are not just our future leaders – they are citizens of today. Their experiences matter. Their ideas matter. Their voices matter. 


If Treaty is truly about creating a better future, then Aboriginal children must remain at the centre of every conversation. 


Because when today’s children become tomorrow’s Elders, they will not judge this generation by the complexity of negotiations or the wording of agreements. 


They will judge us by outcomes. 


Did we create a Victoria where Aboriginal children could grow up proud of who they are? Did we ensure they remained connected to Culture, Country and Community?  Did we reduce the inequities they inherited? Did we create opportunities for every Aboriginal child and their family to flourish and thrive? 


The answers to those questions will be the enduring measure of success. 


So, this Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children’s Day, let us recognise that our children are growing up during a defining chapter in our state’s history, and work together to ensure it’s done right.


We all must take pride in being the first Australian state to take this historic step and ensure that Treaty is not repealed after the state election. 


Because Treaty is a promise to our future generations.  


A promise that they are not simply growing up in the era of Treaty …

author: Nick Reich
title: Introducing the conveners of the Australian Socialist Party: Omar Hassan and Rebecca Barrigos
content:
Over the weekend of 18 July, the Australian Socialist Party was founded. Fledgling as it is, we set ourselves the task of ending an increasingly harsh capitalist system and defeating all the parties who defend that system, from One Nation to the ALP. Achieving that will involve recruiting thousands of socialists to the party, and developing them into activists who can channel the rage of working people into a real force that can win against the odds. 

The Socialist Party’s orientation to its members is unlike any other on the Australian political landscape, where party leaders generally see their members as how-to-vote distribution machines or empty numbers in a faction fight. Socialists aren’t just cheerleaders for parliamentary leaders—our members are fighters. So to help build an active party membership, the Socialist Party founding conference elected two national conveners: Rebecca Barrigos and Omar Hassan.

Both Barrigos and Hassan are teachers and union activists, both have been members of Socialist Alternative since the mid-2000s, both have led impressive campaigns in their home states over the past 20 years, and they’ve each played leading roles in establishing Queensland Socialists and Victorian Socialists respectively. 

Speaking to

Red Flag

, Barrigos remembered the issues that spurred her to join the socialist movement as a uni student:

“The barbarism of the ‘war on terror’, the mass death toll and carnage that was unleashed on the civilian populations of Afghanistan and Iraq, the disgraceful rise of Islamophobia, racism used to justify war crimes, and attacks on civil liberties in the West to quell anti-war opposition, convinced me that I needed to join a socialist organisation that was committed to fighting every institution of the capitalist state.”

Similarly, Hassan related that he “became a socialist in the dark days of the John Howard years, furious at the racism and war that characterised that era”. 

With the resurgence of Hanson’s One Nation and the genocidal wars grinding on in the Middle East, there’s a familiarity to the rage which drove Barrigos and Hassan towards socialism in their youth. The more things change, the more they stay the same.

Sticking it out as socialist activists for two decades, in often difficult circumstances, is an admirable achievement in its own right, but those years meant more than just stubborn principles and passing time for Barrigos and Hassan. They’ve drawn lessons and inspiration from their years of organising. Hassan said that his time on the left has taught him “to appreciate the moments where working-class people come together to fight and win against the system: be it on a small picket line in suburban Melbourne or in mass protests against genocide and imperialism”. 

But mass movements have risen and declined, ebbed and flowed, sometimes scoring small victories but often leaving the fundamental injustice in place. The transience of moments when workers feel their power taught Hassan “how important it is to build a political organisation that can sustain and consolidate the lessons and experiences of those times to build a force that can translate momentum into actual victories”. 

Barrigos made a similar point when speaking about the movement against the Iraq War: “The Iraq War provoked unprecedented resistance. Millions around the world, in Europe, and here in Australia took to the streets in mobilisations even larger than the anti-Vietnam War moratoriums of the 1970s. But despite the size of these rallies, mass protests were never on their own going to stop the US war machine. If we want to win decisively, we need to build a socialist movement that mobilises the power of workers to successfully resist capitalism, and in that fight, lay the basis for a whole different society based on human need, not profit”.

Through their failures and limitations, movements of the past can give their participants a deeper understanding of what’s necessary to win. Not just a firmer conviction, but the right set of politics. Barrigos and Hassan are two among hundreds of experienced socialists who act as conveyor belts for these lessons to a new generation of radicalising young people. There are a few ways they have already been playing this role. They’ve both written insightful theoretical articles for the

Marxist Left Review

 on topics like higher education, the Middle East and Australian politics. They both give impressive speeches.

author: Pip Hinman
title: Will AUKUS keep us safe?
content:
Wollongong Against War and Nukes has joined with many others in this city to show our opposition towards plans to turn our home into a military town. This includes a rally of several thousand people down the main street of Port Kembla in 2023.

As well as more than 40 local organisations, including health and environment bodies, trade unions and church groups, who have signed the Port Kembla Declaration, demanding the federal government rule out a submarine base in our region.

Port Kembla residents have widely opposed having a base in the area and thousands in our community have come together to declare that this is “No Place for a Nuclear Base”.

We are concerned that the presence of nuclear submarines would make the Illawarra a high priority target for conventional or nuclear attack. We are concerned that US submarines carrying nuclear weapons could dock in Port Kembla. We are concerned about the risk of nuclear accidents. We are concerned about becoming a site for the storage of nuclear waste. We are concerned about the social, economic and environmental impact of a nuclear submarine base in Port Kembla. We are concerned that, even in a best-case scenario, a nuclear submarine base would have a highly detrimental impact on our community.

We love Port Kembla and the Illawarra region; we don’t want to lose the things we value about this place.

We have been told that the decision on the location of a nuclear submarine base has been deferred. This is no comfort — if anything it increases our fears that decisions are being made in secret, without community consultation and overriding local dissent.

I take a lot of inspiration from the deep desire for peace that people in our city have shown over many generations. This opposition to war includes the famous “Pig Iron Bob” Dalfram Dispute and, in more recent times, protests against the invasions of Vietnam, Afghanistan and Iraq.

We have repeatedly said “No to war!” For many decades, the local community has also said “No to nuclear war!”

Wollongong was first declared a nuclear-free city in 1980. In 2019, Wollongong City Council signed up to the International Campaign for the Abolition of Nuclear Weapons Cities Appeal. In 2022 and 2025, Wollongong City Council again reaffirmed the city’s nuclear-free status.

Visits or the stationing of nuclear submarines in Port Kembla is seriously dangerous.

Nuclear reactors pose major risks for people and the environment. Unlike civilian reactors, most information about military naval reactors is kept classified. Nuclear-powered submarines have a long history of accidents, many of which are again shrouded in secrecy.

Seven hundred and eighty nine nuclear safety events have been recorded at Scotland’s naval bases since 2006 and the British Ministry of Defence has acknowledged that many incidents had “actual or high potential for radioactive release to the environment”. But it has have refused to say what actually happened in any of the incidents, or when they occurred — raising concerns about whether local residents would be informed if similar incidents occurred in Port Kembla.

Even if the probability of an accident is “low”, the level of consequence of a nuclear submarine accident is extremely high, given that the submarine’s nuclear reactors are fuelled by weapons-grade highly enriched uranium.

The release of secret documents, obtained under FOI legislation in May, demonstrates that planning is being hidden from the public and the risks are being hidden from the communities affected.

Secret NSW government planning documents have considered what should happen in case of an accident or explosion on one of the submarines. Australia’s nuclear safety agency assessed that an accident at a submarine base here would require evacuating most residential streets in Port Kembla. Port Kembla school — the school my two kids attend — would be in the immediate evacuation zone.

Our community has never been properly informed of or consulted about this risk. It is unclear how large the real evacuation zone would be if an accident or an attack on the base occurred. Or for how long the port, or the city, its land, water and air could be contaminated.

Our community knows all about living with a legacy of toxic waste. I have had my garden soil tested for heavy metals and my attic cleaned because of the accumulation of toxic dust over decades. We are already working hard to heal ourselves and the lands and waters we live on. We will not let this …

author: Owen Marsden-Readford
title: Barnaby Joyce—an establishment bigot now serving One Nation
content:
Charles Dickens often created characters whose physical appearance reflected their personal values. Barnaby Joyce, the Akubra-wearing, tomato-red champion of mining and agricultural capital, could have emerged from a Dickens novel set in the VIP section of the horse races. Joyce’s long career in Australian politics is full of scandals and gaffes, including when he was filmed sprawling, drunk, on a Canberra footpath in 2024, or most recently screaming at his dog mid-interview with the ABC. But Joyce is no mere buffoon; he is a calculating politician with strong ties to Australia’s right-wing establishment and some of its most powerful capitalists. 

The recent defection of the former leader of the Nationals and three-time deputy prime minister to One Nation has been an important boost for the surging far-right party. Most notably, Joyce played a vital role in securing Gina Rinehart’s high profile, and lavish, support. The two have enjoyed a long political partnership. Joyce was flying on Rinehart’s private jet as early as 2011. In 2017, Rinehart gave him $40,000 as part of a “champion of farming” award. According to Joyce’s 2018 memoir

Weatherboard and Iron,

it’s a real problem that Australia has only one of her—we need twenty.

Joyce’s role in bringing establishment connections to One Nation has not stopped at Rinehart. In an interview with the

 Saturday Paper

 earlier this year, he bragged: “I can assure you of another thing: she ain’t the only one. I’ve got a lot of substantial supporters and they are approaching me. I don’t have to approach them”. The National Party is dominated by agribusiness, mining capital and rural business owners. Joyce wants to bring his connections to these layers, built over two decades as a leading Nationals powerbroker, to One Nation. He is also crucial to the party’s effort to peel off more of the Nationals membership and voter base.

That Joyce has walked away from his former colleagues in the Coalition and thrown in his lot with Pauline Hanson comes as no great shock. He has long been one of the country’s most prominent far-right figures. 

The Nationals are bitterly hostile to workers and the oppressed, and are the political embodiment of rural reaction. Joyce personified this. He championed every piece of anti-worker legislation and pro-rich policy of the Coalition. He, like much of the Australian right, bemoans “big government” and government interference in the personal lives of citizens. But it’s classic right-wing hypocrisy. Joyce wants mining bosses and farmers to be able to do whatever they like, free from any pesky regulation, yet he consistently argues, and votes, to restrict the rights of workers and the oppressed.

Joyce has always been an odious bigot. In 2006, he opposed adding Gardasil to the vaccination schedule on the basis it would give his then “twelve-year-old daughter a license to be promiscuous”. Gardasil protects women from HPV, which causes 70 percent of cervical cancer cases. Joyce is one of the most vocal opponents of abortion rights in the country, speaking at anti-abortion rallies as both a Nationals and One Nation MP in 2019 and 2026 respectively. He also campaigned against marriage equality.

Joyce was a key opponent of net zero policies within the coalition, fitting his role as mouthpiece for the mining bosses. His hostility to even the most cynical of greenwashing, alongside his relegation to the backbench, was partly behind his shift to One Nation. In 2012, he said even talking about the climate is an “indulgent and irrelevant debate”. In 2019, he posted a

bizarre Christmas Eve video

 claiming that all who do not understand that God is the solution to climate change are “fools” who are “going to get nailed”. He opposes any measures that limit the ability of rich farmers to drain the Murray-Darling for cash crops. This all fits neatly with the drill-baby-drill politics of One Nation.

Joyce has long espoused the politics of racial grievance that is core to One Nation. In

Weatherboard and Iron

 (in which he comes across as equal parts Donald Trump, John Howard and Boggis from

Fantastic Mr Fox

), he paints himself as a champion of poor white people against the woke inner-city elite. Joyce was a prominent part of the racist “No” campaign against the Voice to Parliament. In an

 interview

 with Andrew Bolt, he compared constitutional recognition for Aboriginal people to Nazi race laws, specifically the Civil Service Act of Germany in 1933—one …

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: One thousand parcels in an hour
content:
Millions of parcels are packed and sorted every day inside massive sorting hubs before they reach their destination. Consumers expect their items to arrive in a snap. But this is not simply because of technology – but because of the women workers’ labor inside those massive warehouses. 


By Kat Catalan and Joanna Robles


MARILAO, Bulacan – Online shopping has become part of Filipinos’ everyday lives, growing especially popular during the pandemic. With just one click, a product can arrive at your doorstep in a day or two.


Recent statistics confirm that consumers heavily rely on e-commerce platforms. According to Kepios’

Digital 2026 Philippines

 report, 23.5 million Filipinos shopped online in 2025, with half purchasing from platforms such as Shopee, Lazada, and Temu every week. The most popular products include electronics, food, and clothing.


Studies show that Filipinos trust online shopping platforms because of their affordability, assured product quality, ease of use, and fast delivery.


But what really happens behind the parcels we receive? Whose hands do they pass through? 


Behind every parcel delivery is a woman sorter working under an informal contract, with no protections and, more often than not, no guarantee of receiving her pay by the end of her shift.


On the parcel trackers of online shopping apps, the movement of parcels from sellers’ warehouses to sorting centers can often be seen happening from midnight until the early hours of the morning.


Behind the ‘add to cart’


Joyce (not her real name) formerly worked as a backroom staff at a Shopee hub in Bulacan for six months.


She juggled caring for her six-year-old son while working night shifts inside a sorting center. Before each shift, she patiently waits for her agency to post her schedule on the group chat. Upon arrival at the hub, she lines up alongside workers from various agencies while waiting for the warehouse manager.


There is usually a set number of workers required each day. If she makes the cut, she gets to work and earns P525 for the day. If she does not, she goes home empty-handed, having also spent money on transportation.


Joyce was a worker at SPX Express, the logistics arm of Shopee which is considered the largest e-commerce platform in the Philippines and one of the major companies in Southeast Asia. Kat Catalan/Pinoy Weekly


“There really is no work that isn’t difficult. But inside, you really have to push yourself because someone monitors you with a megaphone. You are not allowed to rest,” Joyce shared with

Pinoy Weekly

. “In an hour, you have to sort 1,000 parcels.”


Work intensifies during sale seasons, when millions of parcels are sorted by around 200 workers in 12-hour shifts. Some workers are even pressured to work overtime with minimal incentives.


Joyce endured this system for months as a solo parent trying to provide for her son. She eventually stopped showing up for work after noticing unexplained deductions in her pay. 


Her agency had been cutting from her wages for “benefits,” yet no contributions were being remitted to her SSS, PhilHealth, or Pag-IBIG accounts. Her frustration peaked when she went home empty-handed after a shift and was even fined for damaged and missing parcels. 


She noted that while management maintains a database of every parcel scanned by each worker, penalties are being imposed arbitrarily.


“What would I even do with those parcels — you can’t take anything out. The guards are very strict. They check everything, even inside your bra and shorts,” Joyce exclaimed. 


Being informal is normal


Alex and Amy (not their real names) are sisters from Camarines Sur. Frequent typhoons and storm surges in their home province pushed them to move to Manila to earn for the family they left behind. After working in various factories over the years, they became parcel sorters in 2025 at a J&T Express


hub, a delivery partner of Shopee and other e-commerce platforms. 


With their years of experience, they have seen their share of workplace abuses, but the treatment inside the hub still shocked them. They have been shouted at and cursed at by supervisors for failing to sort all parcels within eight hours.


From the conveyor belt, sorters separate parcels by the city where they are to be delivered. Alex and Amy handle no fewer than 80,000 parcels in the warehouse each day. Screenshot from a contributed video


“They would shout: ‘The doors are open, you’re free to go. We don’t need you …

In their political resolution, the CPB stated that imperialist intrigues could only be "decisively defeated with AFPFL-CP unity.

However, due to the Burmese independence in 1948, CPB had to re-determine whether AFPFL government (along with the socialists inside it) was a “comprador bourgeoisie” or “national bourgeoisie”.

The Goshal Thesis (On the Present Political Situation in Burma and Our Task) by Thakin Ba Tin (Comrade Goshal) answered this question before CPB as a party had reached a conclusion. As a result, the Goshal Thesis became a political line formulated by Thakin Ba Tin (Comrade Goshal), a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of Burma (CPB), which ignited the sparks of the Burmese Civil War.

The original manuscript of the thesis was discovered in research archives kept in Hamburg, Germany, and was published in 1989 by the Verbund Stiftung Deutsches Übersee-Institut (Hamburg) in a compilation titled Documents on Communism in Burma.

However, Communist Party of Burma (CPB) has been denying the existence of such a thesis. In the November 1992 issue (No. 11) of the CPB’s official journal, ‘People's Power’, an article titled "Clarification Regarding the So-Called Goshal Thesis"—written by Comrade Po Than Gyaung, the current spokesperson of the Communist Party of Burma, with informational assistance from the chairperson of the time, Thakin Ba Thein Tin—argued the following:

title: Bakanlığın alacaklarını ödetme güvencesi verdiği Doruk Madencilik işçileri gözaltına alındı
content:
Çalışma ve Sosyal Güvenlik Bakanlığı'nın iki ay önce taraflar arasında imzalanan protokolle güvence altına alındığını duyurduğu işçi alacaklarının ödenmemesi üzerine yeniden Ankara'ya gelen Bağımsız Maden-İş üyesi Eti Gümüş ve Doruk Madencilik işçilerine polis müdahale etti.


SENDİKA AÇLIK GREVİNDE


ÇSGB: "Doruk Madencilik’te 36 milyon TL ödendi, kalanı haftaya;" Sendika: "Bunlara karnımız tok"


24 Nisan 2026


Enerji ve Tabii Kaynaklar Bakanlığı önünde dört gündür eylem yapan ve alacakları eksiksiz ödenene kadar ayrılmayacaklarını açıklayan işçilerden, aralarında Bağımsız Maden-İş Genel Başkanı Gökay Çakır ile Örgütlenme Uzmanı Başaran Aksu'nun da bulunduğu çok sayıda kişi gözaltına alındı.


Çalışma Bakanlığının verdiği sözler tutulmadı


Madenciler, aylardır ödenmeyen ücret, kıdem ve ihbar tazminatları ile diğer işçilik alacakları için daha önce de Ankara'ya yürümüş, haftalar süren direnişin ardından Çalışma ve Sosyal Güvenlik Bakanlığı'nın devreye girmesiyle eylemlerini sonlandırmıştı. Bakanlık, işçi ve işveren temsilcileri arasında imzalanan protokolün ardından yaptığı açıklamada, işçilerin hak ve alacaklarının belirlenen takvim çerçevesinde ödenmesinin güvence altına alındığını duyurmuştu.


Ancak Bağımsız Maden-İş'e göre aradan geçen sürede bu taahhüt yerine getirilmedi. Elazığ Eti Gümüş'te çalışan 176 işçiden yalnızca yaklaşık 50'sine maaş alacaklarının bir bölümü ödendi; kıdem, ihbar ve emeklilikten kaynaklanan hak edişler ödenmedi. Doruk Madencilik işçilerinin kıdem ve ihbar tazminatları, zorunlu ücretsiz izin dönemlerine ilişkin ücretleri ve bazı işçilerin sendikal tazminatları da hâlâ ödenmedi. Bunun üzerine işçiler bu kez Enerji ve Tabii Kaynaklar Bakanlığı önünde nöbet eylemi başlattı.


Aksu: "Bakanlık bürokratı beş dakika görüşmeyi kabul etmiyor"


Eylemin dördüncü gününde dört işçi, Yıldızlar SSS Holding yetkilileriyle görüşmek üzere Bakanlık önünden ayrıldı. Görüşmeden somut bir sonuç çıkmaması üzerine sendika yöneticileri açıklama yaptı.


Bağımsız Maden-İş Örgütlenme Uzmanı Başaran Aksu, holding yönetiminin önce işçilere borcu bulunmadığını savunduğunu, daha sonra ise sınırlı ödeme yaptığını hatırlatarak, "Holding CEO'su 'Böyle bir şey varsa hemen ödeyeceğiz' dedi. Arkadaşlar görüştü ama olmayan bir uygulama uydurmuşlar. Paraların derhal yatırılması lazım" dedi.


Dört gündür Enerji ve Tabii Kaynaklar Bakanlığı yetkilileriyle görüşme talep ettiklerini ancak hiçbir yanıt alamadıklarını söyleyen Aksu, Bakanlığın sürece kayıtsız kaldığını belirterek şöyle konuştu:


"Tam dört gündür Enerji Bakanlığına, sendika genel başkanımız ve dört-beş madenciyle bir bakanlık bürokratının görüşmesini talep ediyoruz. Bakanlık bürokratı bizimle beş dakikalık görüşmeyi kabul etmiyor. Şeklen de olsa yurttaşla görüşür insan."


Eti Gümüş ve Doruk Madencilik işçileri Enerji Bakanlığı önünde gözaltına alındı


10 Ağustos 2026


İŞÇİLER BAKANLIK ÖNÜNDE


Madenciler hak aramasın diye: Ankara’da 15 gün eylem yasağı


11 Ağustos 2026


Aksu, alacakların tamamı ödenene kadar eylemi sürdüreceklerini belirterek, "Bir daha buraya gelmek istemediğimiz için buradan ayrılmıyoruz. Bakanlık inisiyatif almalı" dedi.


Bağımsız Maden-İş Genel Başkanı Gökay Çakır da yapılan ödemelerin işçilerin haklarını karşılamadığını belirtti:


"Bir işçinin 100 bin lirası varsa 25 bin lirasını ödediler. Patron şimdi 'Paraları ödedik' diyor. Paraları ödeseniz biz buradan gideriz. Bir işçimizin bir lirası kalana kadar sendika olarak buradayız." 


Çakır, dört gündür Bakanlıktan randevu istediklerini hatırlattı:


"En azından işçilerinizi dinleyin. Beş dakika da olsa 'evet' ya da 'hayır' deyin. Biz bu işçileri dinletmeden, bu işçilerin hakkını almadan buradan gitmeyeceğiz." 


Polis madencileri gözaltına aldı


Sendika yöneticilerinin alacaklar ödenene kadar Enerji Bakanlığı önünden ayrılmayacaklarını açıklamasının ardından polis alana müdahale etti. Çevik kuvvet ekipleri basın mensuplarını eylem alanından uzaklaştırırken müdahalenin görüntülenmesini de engelledi. Ardından aralarında Gökay Çakır ve Başaran Aksu'nun da bulunduğu çok sayıda madenci gözaltına alındı. Müdahale sırasında fenalaşan iki işçi ambulansla hastaneye kaldırıldı.


(AEK)

author: Unknown
title: Family Services Workers in Ohio Have Been Striking for Six Months
content:
A sign in the empty parking lot at the administrative offices for Lorain County Job and Family Services (JFS) in Elyria, Ohio, tells passersby that the agency is open for business. That’s only part of the story.


On the perimeter of the empty parking lot in front of the building is a picket line by members of Auto Workers (UAW) Local 2192 who began a strike on February 18. It has become the longest public sector strike in Ohio history, with 140 case workers on strike.


Inside the JFS headquarters are largely empty offices with a growing mass of benefit applications waiting to be processed. Supervisory staff are working extra-long hours but can’t keep up.  Medicaid, food stamps, child support, childcare assistance, adult protective services, and other critical social services managed by JFS are on hold for county residents who desperately need them.


The contract expired last September.  The union’s focus is on chronically low wages, high job turnover rate, and a 50 percent increase in healthcare costs. Among its demands was an annual 8 percent wage increase.


Darlene Gray, a strike captain, said workers can walk through the door at the JFS agency in neighboring Erie County and “make more than I make after working for 23 years at Lorain JFS.”


REJECTED PROPOSALS


The County Commissioners called the union’s contract demands “unrealistic” in the face of budgetary constraints that they claim the county is facing.


The contract dispute was referred to a State Employment Relations Board neutral fact-finder.  But on January 27, the Lorain County Board of Commissioners unanimously rejected the fact-finder’s recommendation for a 3-year contract with wage increases of 4.5 percent, 3.5 percent and 4 percent. The Board urged both sides to continue to bargain.


The county gave a final offer of a 12 percent total wage increase over three years on February 10, and then declared impasse after the county commissioners rejected the union’s proposal for a $1 per hour above the proposal.  While the union expressed a willingness to continue negotiations, the commissioners refused.


Lorain County residents have complained to local news media that they have to wait hours on the phone to reach staff at JFS and experience delays of over a month just to find out if their benefit application was approved. Kathleen Janda, Director of Operations at the Lorain County Free Clinic, told Cleveland NewsChannel 5 that the non-profit has seen an increase in requests for its free pharmacy services from people whose Medicaid coverage has lapsed due to the strike.


Gina Jones, Chair of the union’s bargaining team, lays blame for the strike squarely on the County Commissioners and said that “we’re going to be on strike until we get what we need.”


FISCAL MISMANAGEMENT


She cited public records data that reveal fiscal mismanagement by commissioners that contribute to the county’s budget crunch. According to County Auditor records, six-figure salaried administrative positions at the county zoomed from 55 in 2021 to 174 in 2025.


Jones cited a report by a local independent investigative journalist who

uncovered internal emails

 by one of the commissioners about ways to shield administrative personnel compensation from public scrutiny.


Jones said the union’s $1 supplement wage demand adds up to a small fraction of those

administrative pay hikes

.  Meanwhile, Lorain commissioners have been embroiled in a series of scandals. Earlier this year the commissioners slashed funding to the county emergency children’s shelter. Officials from the County Domestic Relations and Juvenile Court said that they had been by blindsided by the cut and were forced to close the shelter.


In June, the County Sheriff’s Public Corruption Unit seized records from the county administration building in a probe of a contract for the county 911 call center that was approved by the commissioners.


Jones said the strike has begun to take a toll on union members. “Nine have left JFS for other jobs,” she said. She said UAW strike pay is as much or more than JFS workers were being paid for working.


Gray worried about what working conditions will be like for case workers when the strike ends. “We were already short-staffed before the strike, and now there’s a huge backlog of work waiting for us.”


Philip Althouse is a member of UAW Local 2320, and a Senior Attorney at Cleveland Legal Aid.

author: Extremadura Libre
title: Pronto disponible el Extremadura Libre nº 37: noventa años después, seguimos hablando de revolución.
content:
Pronto estará

 disponible el nº 37 de

Extremadura Libre

, correspondiente al verano de 2026

, el periódico de la CNT de Extremadura. Un número que mira de frente a nuestro presente y recupera una historia que sigue siendo incómoda para quienes prefieren una clase trabajadora dócil: la de la

Revolución Social de 1936

 y la capacidad de quienes trabajan para organizarse, decidir y transformar la realidad desde abajo.


La revista arranca con la mirada puesta en el

anarcosindicalismo y la acción sindical

. Hablamos de organización desde los centros de trabajo, de secciones sindicales, de autonomía y de la necesidad de que nadie decida por quienes trabajan. También abordamos luchas concretas: el

indulto a las seis de La Suiza

, la precariedad en la campaña de la cereza y la batalla por unas condiciones dignas para quienes trabajan en el CIAE. Porque los derechos laborales no se regalan: se conquistan organizándonos.


La realidad más dura del trabajo también ocupa un espacio central.

Doce muertes laborales en Extremadura durante 2026

 sirven para denunciar un sistema de prevención insuficiente, controles que no están a la altura y una Administración que sigue llegando tarde.


Desde una perspectiva libertaria, el número entra también en otros frentes de lucha. El

neopatriarcado

, la mercantilización de los cuerpos y las nuevas formas de violencia contra mujeres e infancia muestran que la dominación no desaparece porque cambie de apariencia. Y frente al avance del

neonazismo y la extrema derecha

, recogemos el caso de Cabezuela del Valle y la respuesta necesaria ante quienes pretenden imponer el miedo mientras las instituciones miran hacia otro lado.


Miramos también al territorio. Las

macroplantas de biometano

, como antes las grandes instalaciones fotovoltaicas, plantean una pregunta que el discurso del progreso suele esconder:

¿quién decide sobre nuestros pueblos y quién obtiene los beneficios?

 Frente al modelo que convierte Extremadura en territorio de sacrificio, reivindicamos organización popular, defensa del territorio y capacidad de decisión desde abajo.


La

memoria histórica

 vuelve a ocupar un lugar imprescindible. La revista denuncia el intento de convertir monumentos franquistas en supuesto patrimonio democrático y recuerda que no puede existir una verdadera memoria sin reconocer a quienes sufrieron represión, cárcel y asesinato.


Y hablamos también de

vivienda

, de la nueva aristocracia del ladrillo y de un mercado que convierte un derecho básico en negocio. De inteligencia artificial y de sus promesas, límites y contradicciones. De cultura, flamenco y memoria popular, a través de una entrevista con

Tonio

, un cantaor de nuestra tierra. Recordamos a

Luis Pablo de Torres

, compañero de CNT Mérida recientemente fallecido, cuya vida estuvo dedicada a la libertad. Y nos acercamos a la exposición

La llama, siempre viva, de la Revolución Social

, noventa años después de aquel verano de 1936.


Cerramos con literatura y pensamiento libertario: una mirada crítica al revisionismo en la novela sobre la Guerra Civil y una aproximación a

Rudolf Rocker y Gastón Leval

, dos nombres fundamentales para comprender la teoría y la práctica del anarquismo y el anarcosindicalismo.


Noventa años después, la revolución no es una pieza de museo. Es memoria, pero también pregunta. ¿Qué podemos hacer hoy, juntas y juntos, para dejar de obedecer y empezar a decidir?


Ese es, en el fondo, el hilo que recorre este

nº 37 de

Extremadura Libre

.

Leer, organizarse, luchar y construir desde abajo. Como siempre.


La entrada

Pronto disponible el Extremadura Libre nº 37: noventa años después, seguimos hablando de revolución.

 se publicó primero en

Confederación Nacional del Trabajo

.

Following the recent use of conspiracy charges to successfully convict people in both the Prairieland case in Texas and the Spokane 3 case in Washington, 15 community members in the Twin Cities were indicted on June 16 for resisting the Trump administration’s December 2025 immigration crackdown dubbed “Operation Metro Surge.” According to the indictment, all defendants are identified as “members and associates of … Direct Action Minnesota (‘DAMN’),” which helped organize Minnesota’s resistance. That organization is now defunct in light of the arrests and revelations about government infiltration.

The primary charge against these 15 community members is that each of them “did knowingly conspire, with other persons known and unknown … to prevent by force, intimidation, and threats officers and employees of the United States Department of Homeland Security from discharging the duties of their officers.” Those accused of “conspiracy” are alleged to have done such routine organizing activities as moderating meetings, engaging in fundraising, posting on social media, and communicating on the secure texting app Signal. Some are also accused of participating in an anarchist speaking tour, called “Breaking the ICE: Lessons from the Resistance in Minnesota,” which followed the collapse of the government’s campaign against the people of Minnesota.

title: Antifa-Ost-Prozess: trotz Unterbringung in der Psychiatrie verhandlungsfähig?
content:
Ein weiterer zäher Prozesstag im Dresdner Antifa-Ost-Komplex fand diesen Mittwoch statt. Es ist schon fast 10:30 Uhr, als die wenigen Zuschauer:innen die sich eingefunden hatten, in den Saal dürfen, denn seit gestern war die Öffentlichkeit ausgeschlossen.


Was war passiert?


Einer der Angeklagten befindet sich in einer psychisch sehr belasteten Phase und verliert Lebenskraft sowie Lebensmut. Das zuständige Amtsgericht hat ihn zu seinem Schutz vorläufig in die Psychiatrie eingewiesen, dort darf er nichts besitzen, womit er sich das Leben nehmen könnte, keinen Gürtel, keinee Schnürsenkel, keine Ladekabel.


Dies war vermutlich schon am Tag zuvor in nicht-öffentlicher Sitzung erörtert, die Öffentlichkeit jedoch zum Schutz der persönlichen Belange des Betroffenen ausgeschlossen worden. Jetzt ist es aber sein Anwalt der in der heutigen Sitzung genau diese Details vorträgt, als er ein Obergutachten fordert.


Der eine Arzt der Klinik spricht davon, dass der Betroffene, wenn überhaupt, nur dann reisefähig ist, wenn medizinisches Personal diesen begleitet, ein anderer Arzt wiederum sieht keinerlei Bedenken was Verhandlungs- und Reisefähigkeit angeht.


Auch die Verhandlungsfähigkeit ist strittig, zum einen wegen der akuten Belastungsreaktion und krisenhaften Zuspitzung im Leben des Angeklagten, zum anderen wegen dessen Medikation, denn das verordnete Psychopharmakon wirkt stark dämpfend.


Das Oberlandesgericht lässt den Angeklagten jedoch aus der Psychiatrie nach Dresden bringen, ohne allerdings, dass das polizeiliche Begleitpersonal über die konkrete Situation umfassend informiert ist, ohne dass Notfallmedikamente zur Hand sind, ohne, dass die Polizei weiß was bei welchem Notfall konkret zu tun wäre. Der Anwalt ist ersichtlich empört, auch weil im Gerichtsgebäude sich dieses Unwissen bei den Wachtmeister:innen nahtlos fortsetzt.


Der Antrag wird entgegen genommen, aber eine Antwort einstweilen vom Vorsitzenden zurück gestellt.


Die einzige Zeugin des Tages


Geladen ist Kriminalhauptkommissarin Golze, die knapp eine viertel Stunde über ihre Vernehmung des angeblich geschädigten Neonazi Karl Jonas Kaden befragt wird. Dieser soll in Wurzen 2020 nach seiner Rückreise von einer Demonstration in Dresden, am Bahnhof in Wurzen attackiert worden sein.


Kaden selbst wollte am 19. März 2026 vor dem Oberlandesgericht

nicht aussagen

, er selbst befindet sich gerade in Haft, da er im „Sächsische-Separatisten-Prozess“ als Angeklagter vor Gericht steht.


Und so hangelt sich die Polizistin durch ihre Erinnerungen daran, was der Zeuge Kaden im Rahmen ihrer Vernehmung gesagt haben soll. Sie hätte ihn, nach Rücksprache mit seinen Eltern in dessen Kinderzimmer vernommen, er habe klar auf alle Fragen geantwortet und sich der AfD zugerechnet und als „geschichtsinteressiert“ bezeichnet. Mit ein paar anderen sei er nach Dresden Gefahren, wo jedes Jahr Nazis aufmarschieren um an die Bombardierung Dresdens zu erinnern.


Er sei von 15-20 Vermummten attackiert worden, eine Kopfwunde musste getackert werden. Da ihn jemand einen „Scheiß Nazi“ genannt habe, vermute er „Linke“ hinter dem Angriff. Wenig später wir die Zeugin im allgemeinen Einverständnis entlassen und darf gehen.


Langes Betrachten von Bildern auf dem Monitor


Der Rest des Prozesstages, der erneut von diversen Pausen geprägt war, vergeht damit, dass sich die Prozessbeteiligten und die zu Anfang noch 11, dann sieben und am Ende sechs Zuschauer:innen Fotos ansehen. Um den Prozess zu beschleunigen werden zahlreiche Akten im „Selbstleseverfahren“ eingebracht, sprich alle Beteiligten bekommen Zeit und Gelegenheit Aktenteile selbst zu lesen. Die Bilder jedoch, die müssen „in Augenschein“ genommen werden, in der Verhandlung.


So geht es dann mal in die Wohnung von Lina E. aus dem ersten Antifa-Ost-Prozess, man sieht einen Beutel an einer Türklinke hängen. Oder es werden Observationsphotos gezeigt, wobei hier eine der Verteidigerinnen der Verwertung widerspricht, da die rechtlichen Voraussetzungen für die Observation nicht vorgelegen hätten. author: By L. Cam Anderson, Contributor
title: The Fight Against Google’s Minnesota Data Centers
content:
Mankato, MN — Minnesotans gathered on July 25 in the basement of Mankato’s Grace Lutheran Church for a panel on the hyperscale data centers seemingly popping up across the North Star State.


Roughly 80 attendees from the Mankato area and further filled the underground room, frequently adjusting themselves on metal folding chairs throughout the three hour event as the whirring air conditioner kept the space nearly refrigerated.


Aubree Derkson of Pine Island, who has been heavily involved in the fight against the planned Google data center in her small, rural community of roughly 3,000, was the event’s first speaker. Pine Island is 20 minutes north of Rochester on U.S. Highway Route 52 in southern Minnesota.


Derkson described the work that goes into investigating data center development, a seemingly monumental task when the local government signs non-disclosure agreements, otherwise known as NDAs, with the companies that own and develop them. As a result of such agreements, she has to use roundabout methods to root out project details, including calling utility companies to ask about

new high voltage power lines

 and submitting multiple data requests with different government authorities to build a picture of what’s happening.


“Learn from us,” Derkson said. “Because this is not fun.”


The event, cloistered underground, appeared to drip with a paranoia familiar to conspiracy theorists scanning the horizon for black helicopters through shuttered windows. In this case, however, the conspiracy is not imagined. In both

Pine Island

 and

Hermantown

, the projects were kept secret by all parties involved until they were announced in the Star Tribune

following months of lobbying by Google in the state legislature for favorable conditions

 before any plans were announced.


Beyond hiding entire projects from the community until they are well underway through NDAs, Google and other companies erecting hyperscale data centers across the state and the rest of the country consistently obfuscate environmental impacts and the real effects these facilities have on communities. Hyperscale sites are massive structures housing thousands of servers for cloud computing and generative AI, exceeding 10,000 square feet.


Underscoring the cloak-and-dagger nature of these developments, each was given a codename in advance of Google claiming ownership: Project Loon in Hermantown and Project Skyway in Pine Island.


Smaller data centers, such as the dozen already spread around the Twin Cities, typically have an energy capacity less than 20 megawatts. Hyperscale data centers planned for the state have capacities well above 100 megawatts, with the largest being 400 megawatts with

the

panned Geronimo Power data center the was planned for Nobles County.

 


For scale, 100 megawatts is enough electricity for 100,000 households,

according to the International Energy Agency

.


Notably, Google has not yet revealed the expected power consumption of Project Loon or Protect Skyway. However, the plan for Project Loon includes the generation of 700 megawatts, according to a

presentation delivered by Google

 in May.


“While data centers are hardly new, hyperscale ones are in a different league,” the Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy (MCEA) said in

a June statement regarding a recent court victory against a data center in Faribault

. “They are AI-driven industrial campuses that can consume millions of gallons of water a day for cooling, draw enormous amounts of electricity, generate significant noise and light pollution, and, if enough are built, put serious strain on our state’s already stressed groundwater supply and clean energy goals.”


The opaqueness of these operations when dealing with the public is not due to a lack of knowledge. Rather than figuring such things out on the fly, these things are planned well in advance.


 “They know exactly what’s being built,” Bryan Schneider said during his portion of the presentation. Schneider, who was one of the event’s six speakers, has managed data centers in the past and currently works at the Minnesota State University, Mankato, data center.


“They know every floor tile, every ceiling tile, every light that’s going to be in there. […] They know everything. But if you don’t know about it, it’s being withheld.”

author: Isabel Ortega
title: Expansión de la ultraderecha en América Latina amenaza derechos sexuales y reproductivos
content:
En los últimos años, en América Latina, organizaciones feministas y antipatriarcales han encendido alertas por acciones estatales que amenazan con profundizar la negación de derechos fundamentales para las mujeres y sexodisidencias de la región, mientras observan el crecimiento de grupos de extrema derecha que buscan incidir en la política pública orquestando campañas de desinformación y de desprestigio de las organizaciones feministas.

“[Al lograr la] despenalización en nuestros Estados es cuando empezamos a ver un avance más acelerado del movimiento antiderechos. A partir de una serie de movimientos en todo el país, y en todo el contexto global, estos grupos se han visto fortalecidos”, afirma Angie Contreras, de la organización Vivas y Libres, en México, en entrevista con Avispa Mídia.

Los triunfos electorales de la extrema derecha en la región han acelerado este cercamiento, incorporando a integrantes de movimientos antiderechos en las estructurales estatales, desde donde han posibilitado el cierre de programas y la trasformación ideológica de las instituciones. Esta embestida ha sido particularmente dirigida a desandar los logros de los movimientos por las libertades sexuales y reproductivas de las mujeres.

En este primera entrega, presentamos un panorama del avance de los movimientos de ultraderecha que hoy amenazan la autonomía corporal de las mujeres y sexodisidencias en la región, así como sus estrategias y redes transnacionales de acción. En un siguiente trabajo, trataremos cómo se tejen las redes de los grupos antiderechos en el norte y centro de México, y en una tercera entrega, nos acercaremos a las colectivas de base que resisten a la embestida de la extrema derecha en la región.

La alerta de las colectivas y organizaciones sociales no es infundada. Solo el último año se han presentado distintas iniciativas en el continente que buscan desandar el camino de los movimientos por el derecho a decidir. En Chile, por ejemplo, legisladores de los partidos Nacional Libertario, Republicano y Renovación Nacional presentaron el 7 de julio pasado, una iniciativa de reforma al Código Sanitario que obligaría, en caso de ser aprobada, a que las mujeres que busquen acceder a la interrumpción del embarazo por las tres causales que son legales en el país —es decir, violación, riesgo vital para la madre e inviavilidad fetal— tengan que escuchar el latido fetal como un paso para otorgar el consentimiento para la realización del procedimiento.

Esta iniciativa surge en el marco del primero año de gobierno de José Antonio Kast, quien en el pasado se ha nombrado “defensor de la vida desde la concepción” y desde su campaña anunció su intención de realizar cambios a los programas educativos de Chile, bajo el lema de garantizar una educación “libre de ideologías”.

De igual manera, en Colombia, el 30 de julio, un grupo de legisladores presentó un proyecto de reforma al Artículo 11 de la Constitución, para establecer la protección de la vida “desde la concepción”, como una forma de contrarrestar que en este país el aborto es legal de forma libre hasta la semana 24 de gestación, según fue resuelto por la Corte Constitucional en 2022. Una semana después de la presentación de esta iniciativa, el 7 de julio pasado, asumió el cargo de presidente de Colombia Abelardo de la Espriella, acompañado de otros mandatarios de extrema derecha de la región como Javier Milei, presidente de Argentina, el mismo José Antonio Kast y Daniel Noboa, presidente del Ecuador.

En México, durante este año, legislaciones locales han propuesto, con éxito, declarar el 25 de marzo —día de la Anunciación en el calendario católico— como el “Día del niño por nacer” o “Día de protección a la vida humana”. Esto surge en estados como Nuevo León donde el aborto no ha sido despenalizado completamente, a pesar de que la penalización del aborto fue declarada inconstitucional en México por la Suprema Corte de Justicia de la Nación en septiembre de 2021. Solo por mencionar algunos ejemplos en la región.

Más allá de estas iniciativas legislativas, una tendencia que resulta especialmente preocupante para las organizaciones de la región es del adelgazamiento de las estructuras estatales encargadas de garantizar los derechos sexuales y reproductivos.

Esta tendencia se observa principalmente en países como Argentina donde, de acuerdo al informe El costo de la retirada: Barreas, endeudamiento y desigualdad en el acceso al aborto en Argentina, publicado por Amnistía …

author: Act for freedom now!
title: House Visit for AI Drone Developer and Molotov Attack on Microsoft (Montreal, Canada)
content:
This action targeted the official residence of the founder and the headquarters of Munera Intelligence. Munera develops AI-powered drones that will watch over our streets with AI technology following an agreement with the City of Montreal announced in June. The windows and door of Dominic MacDuff-Auger were destroyed. The City insists that these drones will only be used in construction zones. However, like any camera system, the data they collect will only reinforce the surveillance system that the police are putting in place to cover the entire city. This drone program is part of a wider project that includes the recently announced deployment of cameras powered by AI and managed by the police across all of the city, which aims to normalize growing intrusions into our lives and wage a constant war on our capacity to live in freedom. There is no doubt that if the use of AI drones by the city is allowed to develop, our future will more and more resemble a world where the sky is filled with robots making Amazon deliveries and watching over our total obedience to increasingly authoritarian governments.

The same night, Molotov cocktails were thrown at a Microsoft office. This attack was in response to the quiet expansion of data centers, in which Microsoft plays a major role. Data centers are a key element of contemporary capitalist power. They are at the core of the rise of artificial intelligence, which is destroying the planet and creating new surveillance tools in doing so. Microsoft’s technology, among others, is used by the Israeli government in its campaign of genocide against the Palestinian people. During this attack, challenges were encountered lighting the Molotovs — challenges that did not arise during tests. Be assured, these difficulties will be corrected in the future.

We were told once upon a time that a better future awaited us — a future in which people would have everything they need, water and food would be abundant and healthy, and the air perfectly breathable, in which work would be reduced to the minimum, and people would live without gods nor masters. What happened to this future? Need we simply wait for the science fiction of a 1984, Mad Max, or Blade Runner to become reality, while we serve as guinea pigs for technological sects? No, as long as a revolution is still possible, you know us: we will be there to see it through!

No more mercy. It’s time to declare war on AI, surveillance and their developers! The methods we choose must be on par with the seriousness of our situation: Molotovs, house attacks, and more. We can no longer delay the moment of fighting, struggling, attacking — and so on until total victory. The total victory of the social revolution. The total victory of life. AI must be destroyed!

Better days lie ahead. Long live anarchist revolution!

Revolutionary Anarchist Liberation Front

author: A.N.A.
title: Convocação para uma Semana de Ação Contra o Estado Alemão, de 7 a 13 de setembro de 2026
content:
Para que fique claro: o fascismo está aqui. É hora de parar de seguir a vida com a sensação de estar vendo fantasmas. O fascismo está firmemente enraizado no “status quo” atual, e arrancá-lo pela raiz é a nossa tarefa. Em 6 de setembro, serão realizadas eleições estaduais na Saxônia-Anhalt, um reduto da AfD [partido de direita]. Muitos indícios apontam para a conquista da maioria absoluta pelo partido. Estamos cansados ​​de discutir redução de danos, voto estratégico ou as chamadas práticas democráticas em geral. Independentemente de a AfD vencer ou não, sabemos que as forças autoritárias atuais em todo o mundo ocidental estão se preparando para o fascismo e a guerra. E a Alemanha desempenha um papel importante nisso. Manifestações, correntes humanas e petições não mudarão o sistema; precisamos encontrar outras formas de agir. Faltam três anos para as próximas eleições gerais na Alemanha, e as pessoas que vivem lá precisam se preparar para um governo liderado pela AfD. Queremos discutir e colocar em prática o que é necessário para destruir as engrenagens do Estado. De uma perspectiva anarquista, pode surpreender que estejamos convocando esta semana de ação.


Não queremos cair em um ativismo cego que se oriente excessivamente pela política parlamentar. No entanto, decidimos que este é um bom momento para traçar uma linha divisória. Há inúmeras razões para atacar o Estado alemão. Um Estado em particular tem despertado muita revolta nos últimos anos e, infelizmente, não é a Alemanha. Tem sido inspirador ver perspectivas críticas sobre o estatuto de Estado ganharem força na luta contra o genocídio na Palestina; contudo, elas têm se concentrado quase exclusivamente em Israel. Acreditamos ser importante dedicar grande atenção, em nossa luta, aos Estados sob os quais vivemos; não existe Estado bom. Trata-se de um dos principais impulsionadores do desenvolvimento militar na UE, trabalhando para militarizar sua própria sociedade a uma velocidade vertiginosa. Questionários enviados pelo correio estão coletando informações sobre a capacidade de combate de pessoas registradas como homens em todo o país. A Alemanha tem a ambição de se tornar a maior força militar da Europa… novamente, e conta com boas oportunidades para isso: uma indústria gigantesca e uma economia baseada em salários baixos, o que torna atraentes os empregos no exército e na indústria bélica.


A infraestrutura civil e a “economia da paz” servem de base para a infraestrutura de guerra. A história da Alemanha nos lembra bem que nossos queridos trens são cruciais para o transporte de tropas, armas, recursos e prisioneiros por longas distâncias. Empresas que fabricam, por exemplo, máquinas industriais simples, eletrônicos ou peças de precisão para a indústria automotiva frequentemente integram cadeias de suprimentos militares. Hoje, praticamente todas as grandes cidades abrigam algum tipo de indústria militar — desde a produção de armas e equipamentos de radar até o desenvolvimento de drones. É hora de agir. A Alemanha vem caminhando em direção ao fascismo na última década (assim como muitos outros Estados), e não há dúvidas quanto a isso. Independentemente de qual partido vença as eleições de 6 de setembro, fascistas assumirão posições de ainda mais poder. Eles começarão a alterar a legislação e a atacar e denunciar publicamente todo tipo de projeto ou organização de caráter liberal ou emancipatório.


Eles prepararão o terreno para abusos, punições, agressões físicas e a criminalização de pessoas marginalizadas. Eles fomentarão o Estado policial e a censura. Já começaram, mas não se engane: após 6 de setembro, haverá pouca ou nenhuma chance de deter o fascismo por meio do Estado, pois eles próprios — ainda mais do que antes — serão o Estado. O que faremos depois de 6 de setembro? Acreditamos na escolha criteriosa de nossos alvos, levando em conta o impacto que isso possa ter na vida das pessoas que dependem deles. Sob um governo fascista, cada repartição pública e cada funcionário estatal fazem parte do sistema e o apoiam. Isso significa que, após a eleição, toda a infraestrutura do Estado — mesmo aquela aparentemente irrelevante — integra o governo fascista e, portanto, torna-se um alvo legítimo: cadeias, presídios, órgãos governamentais, agências de emprego, delegacias de polícia, quartéis, departamentos de registro de estrangeiros… Há alvos suficientes por aí. Les identitaires européens de la campagne raciste

Save Europe Act

 organisent une tournée européenne pour propager en toute impunité leur projet de durcissement des politiques migratoires et de «

 

remigration

 

» c'est-à dire littéralement la déportation des personnes immigrées. Ce projet ne surgit pas dans le vide. Partout en Europe, les politiques migratoires se durcissent, les discours racistes se banalisent, ce qui était hier porté par les marges de l'extrême droite est aujourd'hui repris dans les discours politiques et médiatiques et se traduit dans les politiques publiques. Le Parlement européen a adopté en mars un texte ouvrant la voie à un renforcement des procédures d'expulsion, à la possibilité de recourir à des «

 

plate formes de retour

 

» et à l'utilisation accrue des centres de rétention administratifs.


La déshumanisation des personnes migrantes se banalise, entraînant une multiplication des agressions racistes, comme à Belfast où des milices d'extrême droite ont attaqué et incendié des maisons de familles immigrées. Pendant ce temps, les frontières européennes continuent de tuer. Quand les voies légales sont fermées, celles et ceux qui cherchent refuge sont contraintes de prendre des routes toujours plus dangereuses. À Ceuta comme en Méditerranée, les morts et les drames humains se succèdent. Et à chaque nouvelle tragédie, l'extrême droite réclame davantage de frontières alors que celles-ci sont déjà bien verrouillées.


Nous refusons cette logique, d'autant plus si l'on tient compte de la responsabilité de l'Etat français dans ces mouvements migratoires, à travers son soutien aux projets coloniaux et impérialistes, sa complicité aux crimes de guerres et génocides et son inaction face à la crise climatique. L'internationalisme demeure la meilleure réponse au nationalisme et la libre circulation des personnes est la seule réponse désirable aux questions migratoires. Après Utrecht aux Pays-Bas où les fascistes ont pu parader, puis Lille où leur rassemblement a été annulé par la préfecture, et avant de passer en Espagne où ils vont continuer d'instrumentaliser le drame humanitaire de Ceuta à des fins racistes, les fascistes prévoient de venir déployer leur banderole «
