author: CNT Galiza
title: Paco Ponzán: anarcosindicalismo, revolución y resistencia
content:
La vida de Francisco Ponzán Vidal (Oviedo, 30/03/1911 – Buzet-sur-Tarn, Francia, 17/08/1944) revela el compromiso constante del movimiento anarquista ibérico con la transformación de la sociedad, antes y después del golpe de Estado franquista, así como con la lucha antifascista, que aún hoy conserva gran relevancia. Maestro de profesión, militante de la CNT y destacado organizador anarquista, Ponzán centró su vida en la revolución social y la solidaridad internacional, tanto durante la Guerra Civil como posteriormente en la Resistencia francesa contra el nazismo.


Aunque nació en Oviedo, su familia pronto se trasladó a Huesca. Allí creció y, años más tarde, influenciado por la biblioteca de su padre y las conversaciones con un profesor, conoció a Ramón Acín, figura histórica de la CNT en Huesca, quien lo introdujo en el pensamiento anarquista. Esta intensa amistad perduró hasta 1936, año en que Acín y su compañera, la también anarquista Concha Monrás, fueron torturados y fusilados por los fascistas.


Desde muy joven, Ponzán participó en el Ateneo Cultural Libertario de la ciudad. Estudió magisterio, título que obtuvo con apenas dieciocho años. Su primer trabajo como maestro lo llevó al pueblo de Ipas, cerca de Jaca, donde vivió de cerca el clima político de la Segunda República en la región. En diciembre de 1930, se produjo el levantamiento republicano contra la monarquía corrupta, conocido como el Levantamiento de Jaca, liderado por los capitanes Fermín Galán y Ángel García Hernández, que marcó el inicio de una fuerte escalada represiva contra los militantes revolucionarios. A partir de entonces, las detenciones de Ponzán por la policía y la guardia civil se hicieron cada vez más frecuentes debido a su participación en huelgas y movilizaciones obreras.


Enviado a Mazaricos en 1934, al principio la distancia le dificultó el contacto con sus camaradas de la CNT de La Coruña; pero el problema se resolvió en febrero de 1936 con su traslado a Camelle, donde se unió al grupo de Noia. Las notas del sacerdote de Ponte do Porto, quien seguramente lo envidiaba, datan de este período, pues anota sobre Ponzán: «

Hace exactamente un año que organizó, con el conocimiento y la paciencia de las autoridades, una procesión religiosa precedida por él, en burla del día del Espíritu Santo en Camelle

». Estas palabras se añadieron poco después a otras notas en su expediente de purga, donde se le acusa de ser una «

persona muy peligrosa» que «estuvo a punto de llevarnos hacia un sovietismo libertario local

» e incluso de ser «

más amigo de los explosivos que de los libros de texto para la enseñanza

». Entre el delirio y la crueldad de estas notas, se puede reconocer, al menos, que demuestran no solo el grado de cobardía de quienes, poco después, iban a asolar el país, sino también la capacidad organizativa de una clase obrera con una conciencia cada vez más crítica.


El golpe militar de julio de 1936 lo sorprendió en Huesca, donde había ido a pasar sus vacaciones tras adelantarlas, pues ya percibía un ambiente general preocupante. La ciudad fue tomada inmediatamente por los golpistas, por lo que tuvo que huir a territorio republicano.


Allí, Ponzán asumió responsabilidades políticas dentro de las instituciones creadas por el movimiento anarquista en Aragón, en una experiencia singular de autogobierno promovida por la CNT, basada en la colectivización de la economía, la democracia directa y la organización popular. Fue primero Ministro de Transportes y Comunicaciones en el Consejo Regional de Defensa y posteriormente se incorporó a la Subsecretaría de Información y Propaganda del Consejo de Aragón, dirigida por el también anarquista Evaristo Viñuales.


Con el avance de la guerra, la tensión entre las organizaciones revolucionarias y los sectores partidarios de la centralización del poder se intensificó progresivamente. El PCE, fortalecido por la ayuda soviética, optó por militarizar las milicias y subordinar la revolución a los objetivos militares de la República. Por el contrario, la CNT y el POUM defendieron una revolución social inseparable de la lucha contra el fascismo.


El enfrentamiento alcanzó su punto álgido en los sucesos de mayo de 1937 en Barcelona. Ponzán participó en la defensa de las posiciones anarquistas durante los combates callejeros hasta que fue arrestado por las fuerzas comunistas. Incluso fue llevado al pelotón de fusilamiento, del que logró escapar gracias a otros militantes anarquistas. El posterior …

author: Unknown
title: Almanya’da ırkçı AfD partisi bir eyalette iktidara yürüyor
content:
Fotoğraf: Oxfordian Kissuth/Wikimedia

Önümüzdeki eylül ayında Almanya’nın dört eyaletinde sandık kurulacak. 6 Eylül’de doğu eyaleti Saksonya-Anhalt, 13 Eylül’de Aşağı Saksonya eyaletleri sandık başına gidecek. 20 Eylül’de ise başkent ve aynı zamanda eyalet olan Berlin’de ve ülkenin kuzeydoğu eyaleti Mecklenburg-Vorpommern’de seçimler gerçekleştirilecek.

Saksonya-Anhalt seçimlerinde ırkçı parti AfD’nin önde olması ve ilk defa bir eyalette yönetime gelmesi ihtimali ise tartışma yarattı. DW Türkçe’nin haberine göre anketler AfD’nin oyunun yüzde 42’ye kadar yükseldiğine işaret ediyor.

Bu eyalette “kesinleşmiş aşırı sağ aşırılıkçı grup” olarak sınıflandırılan parti, Almanya genelinde de “aşırı sağ aşırılıkçılık” şüphesiyle istihbarat örgütü olan Anayasayı Koruma Teşkilatı’nın gözetimi altında. Partinin gençlik oluşumu ise federal düzeyde “aşırı sağ” olarak sınıflandırılmıştı.

Saksonya-Anhalt’ta AfD’nin sandıktan birinci parti olarak çıkması halinde ilk kez iç istihbarat teşkilatı tarafından “kesin olarak aşırı sağcı” olarak sınıflandırılan bir parti bir eyalet seçiminde zaferini ilan etmiş olacak.

Ancak AfD’nin tek başına iktidara gelmesi, yalnızca oy oranına bağlı değil. Parti mutlak çoğunluğu sağlayamazsa seçimlerden birinci çıksa bile muhalefette kalabilir.

Saksonya-Anhalt’ta 2002 yılından bu yana iktidara gelen tüm eyalet başbakanları, Başbakan Friedrich Merz’in partisi CDU’dan çıktı. Eyalette halen CDU, Sosyal Demokrat Parti (SPD) ve Hür Demokrat Parti’den (FDP) oluşan koalisyon iktidarda. Eyalet parlamentosuna girmesi beklenen partilerin tamamı, AfD ile birlikte hükümet kurmayı reddettiğini belirtiyor. Bu nedenle hükümet kurma sürecinin zorlu geçmesi bekleniyor.

Nüfusu yaklaşık 2 milyon 100 bin olan Saksonya-Anhalt’ta genç nüfusun oranı oldukça düşük. Eyaletteki yaş ortalaması 2024 yılında 48,3 olarak kaydedildi. Almanya genelinde ise aynı yıl için ortalama yaş 44,9 olarak kayıtlara geçmişti. Yaklaşık 25 milyar avro kamu borcu bulunan Saksonya Anhalt, kişi başına düşen kamu borcu açısından Almanya’nın geniş yüzölçümlü eyaletleri arasında üst sıralarda yer alıyor. 65.5’lik istihdam oranı ise Almanya ortalamasının üzerinde bulunuyor.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Mekong Review 2
title: Stand and fight Calum Stuart
content:
Credit: Ivan Weiss


T

he day I interviewed Daniel York Loh, there was news of anti-immigration protests—some of which turned violent—erupting across Belfast, Northern Ireland. The BBC reported that people had been targeted simply for having “a different skin colour”.


In recent years, xenophobic and racist rhetoric has been on the rise in the UK. This has manifested alongside right-wing politicians and political parties (such as Nigel Farage, leader of Reform UK, and Tommy Robinson, a far-right activist) moving from fringe entities into mainstream influence. For Loh—an actor, writer, and filmmaker of Singaporean and British heritage who has been a vocal supporter of left-wing causes—these developments have been equal parts alarming and maddening.


Based in London, Loh has been working in the performing arts in both the UK and Asia for more than forty years. In that time, he’s become increasingly invested in working to improve Asian representation on stage and on screen. He was a founding member of BEATS (British East and Southeast Asian in Theatre and on Screen), a not-for-profit, volunteer-based advocacy group for British East and Southeast Asians working in theatre, film, or television. He’s also a member of the Race Equality Committee of Equity, the trade union for performers and creatives in the entertainment and performing arts industry. In 2016, he was one of twenty-one contributors to the anthology

The Good Immigrant

, reflecting on issues of race, immigration, identity, and Othering in the UK. A tenth anniversary issue of the book was launched this year.


More recently, Loh appeared in the true crime drama

I Fought The Law

, a four-part series following the determined struggle of Ann Ming—played by the award-winning British actor Sheridan Smith—a former nurse who campaigned for seventeen years to overturn the UK’s double jeopardy law after the murder of her daughter in 1989. Loh stars as Ming’s mixed-race husband, Charlie, in a story that examines grief and trauma, while not shying away from the racial politics of Britain in the 1980s and 1990s.


I’d like to start with

I Fought The Law

, which was based on a true story. It received rave reviews and you were nominated for an award at the 2026 Royal Television Society North East and the Borders Awards. What was it like taking on this role and playing a character based on a real person?


Daniel York Loh with Sheridan Smith in I Fought The Law. Credit: Anastasia A Arsentyeva


Charlie Ming, he was like me. He was mixed race but, essentially, very, very British. Very, very Middlesbrough [a town in North Yorkshire, England]. Ann Ming was kind of an advisor on the series, but [Charlie’s] not around anymore.


I Fought The Law

 was based on Ann Ming’s book [

For the Love of Julie

, published in 2009]. It was a real privilege to do it. It was such a good script and an amazing story. Sheridan Smith is an amazing actor and we had a great director [Erik Richter Strand]. I can’t speak highly enough of the whole thing, really.


I got the impression that it resonated with people because, right now, there’s a widespread sense of cynicism in many places. But in the series you have an ordinary person who’s taking on a massive system and prevailing.


I’m told the viewing figures were very high for the modern era. I think people were very taken with [the story]; it was a genuinely huge achievement. Ann Ming kept on going, she was very dogged, which I think people really admire… when you win in the end. If you’re very dogged and you don’t win, they kind of think you’re mad.


How do you feel the series dealt with the issue of racism?


There was a scene that flashed back to when Ann and Charlie were younger, and the racist neighbour comes around and there’s graffiti with racist slurs on the wall outside. And there were a few people online going, “Oh, typical ‘woke’ ITV.” But that’s in her book! It’s in Ann Ming’s book, and it was actually much worse. They suffered terrible racism when they first got together. I wanted that stuff in there. It’s important in social history and it resonates with what’s going on now.


There’s always people who want to blame migrants for anything and everything. If you put one foot out of line, your entire ‘community’—in inverted commas, because people don’t know each other a lot of the time—suffers. It reminds me of my own childhood. My childhood was basically [full of] racist abuse and my dad coming up to the school; the teachers …

author: Mag
title: Am autoritären Kipppunkt: „Law and Order“-Politik hat Konjunktur
content:
Dossier


„… In der Klimaforschung ist ein Kipppunkt ein Moment, an dem – laut Weltklimarat – „eine kritische Grenze“ erreicht wird, „jenseits derer sich ein System umorganisiert“, neue Prozesse sich verfestigen und negative Dynamiken sich beschleunigen. Dies lässt sich auch auf gesellschaftliche Kipppunkte übertragen. Kipppunkte entstehen nicht zufällig, sie sind das Ergebnis länger zurückliegender destruktiver Prozesse. Doch im Gegensatz zum Klima sind gesellschaftliche Prozesse nie unumkehrbar. Allerdings sind etablierte Diskurse, Strukturen und Normen oft nicht rückgängig zu machen. Sind autoritäre Kipppunkte überschritten, wird der Boden brüchig, auf dem plurale und demokratische Gesellschaften stehen…“

Kommentar von Daniel Mullis, Maximilian Pichl und Vanessa E. Thompson vom 16. Juni 2023 in der taz online


, siehe mehr daraus und dazu:


[Buch: »Erziehung zur Grausamkeit. Die Massenpsychologie des Neuen Faschismus«] Lehrjahre der Unmenschlichkeit: Faschismus als Prozess der Verrohung


„

Seit dreißig Jahren, in manchen Nationen sogar schon länger, erleben wir einen Aufstieg des rechten Populismus. Ultrarechte Parteien werden nicht nur stärker, viele radikalisieren sich auch nach und nach – oder sogar rasend schnell. Und eine entscheidende Rolle spielt dabei ein Kult der Härte, der die schräge Allianz aus Neuem Faschismus und Ultraliberalen fest zusammenhält.


Konnte man vor einigen Jahren noch vom aufkommenden »Rechtspopulismus« sprechen, wäre das heute in vielen Fällen eine Verharmlosung. Rechtsextremismus oder Neuer Faschismus trifft es da schon weit besser, bedenkt man, dass sich faschistische Bewegungen durch eine Reihe von Eigenschaften auszeichnen: Führerkult, paranoide Weltbilder, die permanent geschürt werden, ein Schwarz-Weiß-Denken, antagonistische Feindbilder, vor allem von Minderheiten, aber auch gegen vermeintliche innere Feinde. (…)


Faschismus ist, so gesehen, eher eine Stimmung, die einen nach und nach erfasst und überwältigt. Die Affekte von Gekränktheit, Angst, Neid, das Ressentiment und die Erlösungssehnsucht, sie alle sind ansteckend – und diese Ansteckung läuft nicht bloß von den Agitatoren zu den Anhängern, sondern wirkt kreuz und quer. Wie bei Synapsenverschaltungen werden die Verbindungen gestärkt, je intensiver sie benutzt werden. Emotionen, Tonfall und Phrasen werden übernommen, steigern sich zu Fanatismus.

Der Faschismus ist demnach weniger eine Ideologie als ein sozialer Prozess. Ansteckung ist kein Zufall, sie gedeiht in Milieus, in denen Gefühle zirkulieren wie ein Echo, das lauter zurückkehrt, als es ausgesendet wurde. Bis der Fanatiker am Ende als normal erscheint und der Normale als verdächtig.


Das trifft alles auf Parteien wie die MAGA-Bewegung der US-Republikaner zu, genauso auf die Alternative für Deutschland oder die Freiheitliche Partei in Österreich. Sie alle haben sich in den vergangenen Jahren in einem Prozess der Selbstradikalisierung markant verwandelt. Gewiss, Rechtspopulismus ist nicht dasselbe wie Faschismus, aber die Übergänge sind fließend. Wer als Rechtspopulist begann, kann als Faschist enden.


Und es geschah und geschieht dabei auch etwas Eigentümliches, das bis heute erst in Ansätzen verstanden wird: Die Radikalisierung der einen Partei wirkte als Aufschaukelung und Vorbildeffekt auf die anderen zurück. Das Resultat ist die Radikalisierung aller in einem längst globalen Resonanzraum. Simpel gesagt: Ohne Trump wäre die AfD wahrscheinlich gemäßigter, die FPÖ wäre ohne die AfD weniger radikal – und umgekehrt. (…)


Das ist das Neue an den neuen Rechtsradikalen: Sie können das Weiße Haus erobern, das mächtigste Amt der Welt, sie können beide Parlamentskammern kontrollieren, das höchste Gericht mehrheitlich mit Loyalisten besetzen und das Silicon Valley auf ihrer Seite haben – und betrachten sich noch immer als Widerstandskämpfer gegen eine »linke Hegemonie«. Dafür müssen sie nur Wohlerzogenheit, Respekt und die allgemein anerkannte Sittlichkeit als »links« ansehen. Der Spott über Behinderte wird dann geradezu zur gegenkulturellen Provokation. (…)


Der Rechtsradikale posiert als Widerstandskämpfer gegen den Mainstream – sogar dann, wenn er im mächtigsten Amt sitzt, das es in der Welt zu ergattern gibt. Der Rechtsradikale fühlt sich chronisch unterdrückt – meist durch die Tatsache, dass auch Menschen mit anderen Ansichten existieren – und zugleich mit einer höheren Macht im Bunde. (…)


Während sich die USA daranmachen, allmählich und rasant eine …

author: Sharon Zhang
title: White House Reportedly Lobbied to Keep Accused Abuser Rep. Max Miller in Race
content:
One official suggested that Miller staying in the race seemed inevitable after he compared himself to Trump.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

In the days before the Ohio deadline for candidates to be replaced, the White House waged a campaign to ensure that alleged abuser Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) stayed in his race for reelection, reportedly effectively telling Republicans to “back off” of criticisms of his candidacy.

Politico reported on Monday, citing three sources, that Donald Trump’s political team told Republicans in Ohio in the past week not to publicly criticize Miller. They reportedly said it would “complicate messaging” if Miller stayed in the race and they would then still have to back him — less concerned, seemingly, about the complications that now arise from their backing of a man accused of abusing his ex-wife and their daughter.

An Ohio Republican involved in the discussions told Politico that the White House “basically told us to back off … and let the voters decide.”

Ohio Republicans had reportedly discussed scheduling a meeting to replace Miller, but the White House advised against it, saying that he wasn’t going to drop out and that they wouldn’t be able to find a replacement.

One White House official even told Politico that Miller’s staying in the race seemed inevitable after the House representative compared his situation to the sexual assault allegations against Trump.

Miller has been insistent that he is staying in the race and on Monday surpassed the deadline to be replaced. He is running for reelection against Democrat and union ironworker Brian Poindexter.

Miller has been facing calls to resign ever since allegations came to light earlier this year that Miller once threw boiling water at his ex-wife, held a gun to her head, and fractured their 2-year-old daughter’s collarbone. The ex-wife in question is Emily Moreno, the daughter of Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno (Ohio).

Since the initial allegations, more disputes have come out, including that Miller recently refused to hand over his daughter’s beloved stuffed bunny for 48 hours, and that Miller accidentally shared pictures online of his daughter that some said could be considered child sex abuse material.

Republicans have largely been mum about Miller despite the allegations. Only a handful of Republicans have called for him to resign or withdraw, including his former father-in-law. Meanwhile, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana) said last week that it’s not his “business” to be involved in “domestic events” with his members.

Many within the party believe that Miller will still win the election despite the allegations because Trump won the district by 11 points in 2024.

“It’s still winnable, it’s just going to be expensive,” one Republican told Politico.

Indeed, Politico polling recently found that most Trump supporters say they would still vote for a Republican candidate through numerous scandals. This includes if they were photographed wearing blackface (74 percent); accused of domestic violence (72 percent); or were accused of sexual assault (66 percent).

title: and my take today is that framing misogynistic writing as an “inability to write female characters”…
content:
hierophagy

:

and my take today is that framing misogynistic writing as an “inability to write female characters” subconsciously takes away most of the blame, implying that women are an alien creature compared to men and that it is no fault of the writer because it’s out of their skill set. it’s not an inability, not a lack of expertise, it’s the simple refusal to consider women as individual people and give them the same depth and grace that comes easily to the writer when they write male characters. it’s not that christopher nolan, stephen king, james cameron (and frankly anyone using the argument, both professional and hobbyist; yes, that includes fanfic writers) etc can’t write women, it’s that they just won’t. at that point in time it is a conscious decision driven by the laziness to unpack their misogynistic biases, and should be addressed as such

author: Mosha Folger
title: Sanirajak man sentenced to four and a half years for sex crimes
content:
After a series of delays, Simeonie Issigaitok has received a four-and-a-half year sentence in a federal penitentiary for sexually touching children under the age of 16.


Court staff brought the 73-year-old Sanirajak man from into an Iqaluit courtroom Tuesday in a wheelchair. Through an interpreter, he listened expressionless, occasionally nodding his head, as Justice Christian Lyons read his sentence.


“Vulnerability of Inuit children and, in particular Inuit girls, is demonstrated by the persistent and troublingly high per capita rate of child sexual abuse in Nunavut,” Lyons said. “A problem that Mr. Issigaitok has repeatedly and substantially contributed to for decades.”


Issigaitok pleaded guilty in December 2025 to two counts of sexual interference. The first offence occurred in Sanirajak sometime between 1987 and 1989. Issigaitok assaulted a girl in her early teens at her home while her parents were asleep.


The second incident occurred in April 2021. Issigaitok was captured on security video during a community event touching a boy while he was seated with a group of children.


On Tuesday, Lyons said aggravating factors included Issigaitok’s history of convictions for sex crimes dating back to  which dates back to 1988, his 2014 designation as a dangerous offender, and that his victims were Inuit children.


He also said that he considered the fact that Issigaitok attended residential school, where he was sexually abused, a mitigating factor, as well as Issigaitok’s guilty plea, which meant the victims did not have to testify.


Another mitigating factor was that one of the crimes occurred before the first of his 27 lifetime convictions. Therefore, the court could treat it as a first offense.


“This is attenuated somewhat by the fact that Mr. Issigaitok was abusing other children during the period of the offense and had committed a serious sexual assault a few years prior, for which he was sentenced in 1997,” Lyons said.


Crown prosecutors had sought a 10-year sentence, while defence lawyer Alan Regel argued that his sentence should be for time served in jail while his case worked its way through the legal system. Judges usually credit defendants with one and a half days for every day they spend in pre-trial custody. That means Regal was asking for a sentence of about 21 months.


Lyons sentenced Issigaitok to three years for the crime committed in 1988 and one and a half years for the crime committed in 2021.


Issigaitok will remain at the Aaqqigiarvik Correctional Healing Facility in Iqaluit while he awaits his transfer to a federal penitentiary to serve the two years and nine months left in his sentence.


The sentencing saw two delays. In June, Lyons

delayed the proceeding

 to allow time for one victim to submit a statement. In July, Issigaitok was medevaced to Ottawa because of respiratory problems.


There was one more delay, of about an hour, on Tuesday. The scheduled court interpreter was not in town, and court staff needed to videoconference a new one.

author: Pip Hinman
title: Domestic violence isn’t a ‘two-way street’ and Hanson isn’t confused
content:
Pauline Hanson told Brisbane’s 4BC radio on July 21 that domestic violence is “wrong, but it’s also a two-way street“. She attributed it to the “pressures of living” and said “women can lose their cool as well”.

Fellow One Nation Senator Barnaby Joyce had used the same program earlier that day to advise men to “walk out of the house” before losing their temper, reaching for James Bond as a model of masculine self-control . Brittany Higgins called the framing atrocious, given at least 38 women had already died so far this year at the hands of men. Advocates point out that “just leave” ignores everything known about the danger of separation.

All that criticism is accurate but none explains why “two-way street” sounds true to people who aren’t invested in gender politics. Hanson isn’t inventing this belief. She’s surfacing one that already exists and giving it a slogan; the response to her keeps stopping at her character instead of asking why the slogan lands.

When the backlash built, Hanson posted that she’d been “taken out of context” and that rival media had “used only a few quotes” to make it look like she’d downplayed domestic violence. It’s worth checking, because a genuine misquote reads better in full. The longer version of her comments adds that women “shouldn’t put up with it” if they don’t feel safe at home, the same advice already covered, restated with softer framing rather than corrected.

There’s no context in which “two-way street” becomes something other than what it says. It’s a reflexive move, not a considered one.

Days earlier, when her comments on a podcast about the White Australia policy drew criticism, her daughter went on Sky News to say Hanson had been “taken out of context” there too. Hanson largely let others front the cameras.

Whatever the specific claim, her response is identical: not a correction, but an accusation that the record is being distorted.

Hanson’s cost-of-living framing doesn’t just shift violence onto an external stressor, it states plainly that hitting a partner is a legitimate response to stress. Nearly a quarter of the country already agrees: the 2021 National Community Attitudes towards Violence against Women Survey (NCAS) found 23% of respondents believe domestic violence is “a normal reaction to day-to-day stress and frustration”.

This is not a new position for Hanson. In 2019, as deputy chair of a parliamentary family law inquiry, she told ABC radio that women were “nothing but liars” who fabricate abuse allegations to gain leverage in custody disputes, a claim she couldn’t substantiate beyond her own son’s case. On this one she has real company: 37% of NCAS respondents agreed that women going through custody battles often make up, or exaggerate, claims of domestic violence to gain tactical advantage.

Her “two-way street” view only holds together if domestic violence is real, but that recognition survives only in the abstract. When a specific woman describes her own experience of it, Hanson’s position flips: she becomes someone probably lying, using it, weaponising it against a father.

Domestic violence is real in the abstract, real enough to build a slogan on, and suspect every time an actual woman describes it. That isn’t a contradiction Hanson has failed to notice; it’s the anti-feminist mechanism.

That two-sidedness belief has been getting more common, not less. The same NCAS found 41% of respondents believe domestic violence is equally committed by men and women, and that only 57% recognise men as the predominant perpetrators, down from 74% in 2009.

That’s not evidence the belief has simply always been there, immune to effort. Attitudes towards gender inequality and sexual violence both improved significantly over the same period, so shifting public belief clearly works. It means that whatever has been pulling in the other direction on domestic violence specifically has been working too; figures like Hanson and the wider manosphere ecosystem of influencers and forums that have spent the same period normalising grievances against women.

Hanson’s comments are one part of that pull, not a stray remark landing on inert ground.

There are also documented ways this data gets misread, and setting them out doesn’t vindicate her framing. It explains why the misreading is available for her to use.

While the vast majority of violence orders issued in Australian jurisdictions are issued against men, women do have orders made against them too, and that’s the …

author: rti_admin
title: Selective Ritual Reform and Buddhist Marriage Among Ambedkarites in Odisha
content:
Abstract: Marriage rituals in South Asia have historically reinforced caste and gender hierarchies. Within contemporary Ambedkarite Buddhist communities in Odisha, debates over “mixed marriages” frequently centre on visible Hindu practices such as Brahmin priests, sindur , and the mangalsutra . Drawing on Ambedkarite social media discussions, wedding practices, B. R. Ambedkar’s writings, and anthropological studies of marriage, this article argues that such critiques are often selective. While many Ambedkarites reject Brahmanical symbols, they continue practices such as the baraat , engagement rituals such as Nadia Dhara ( ring ceremonies), status matching in partner selection, and competitive wedding display. These practices reproduce caste, gender, and status hierarchies in new forms. This article argues that Ambedkarite Buddhist marriage remains an evolving social project. Its transformative potential depends on changing the social relations that organise marriage, not simply replacing Brahmanical symbols. It calls on Dalit Bahujan communities to reimagine Buddhist marriage as an ethical practice grounded in equality, solidarity, and collective uplift.

Introduction: Hindu marriage has often been understood as a religious and soteriological event embedded within broader moral and ritual frameworks (Harman, 1987). At the same time, marriage has historically operated as a key social institution through which caste, gender, and hierarchy are regulated and reproduced (Ambedkar, 1916/1979). As Ambedkar argued, the endurance of caste rests significantly on the regulation of marriage, particularly through endogamy and the control of women’s mobility and sexuality. Rituals surrounding marriage are therefore not incidental cultural practices but central mechanisms through which social order is maintained, reproduced, and publicly displayed.

However, marriage also carries the potential for transformation, especially within communities committed to equality and social justice. In the context of Ambedkarite marriage, it becomes a critical site for practising dignity, equality, and mutual respect. At the same time, inherited caste and patriarchal structures can continue to persist in new forms within intimate relationships. It is within this tension between reproduction and transformation that the significance of marriage must be understood. For Ambedkar, challenging caste required transforming both political institutions and everyday social practices that maintain caste boundaries.

The mass conversion to Buddhism in 1956 formed part of this broader social project. Conversion signified a rejection of Brahmanical religious authority, and an embrace of an ethical framework based on equality and rationality (Ambedkar, 1957). Yet the question of how marriage is practised within Ambedkarite communities remains open.

In recent years, debates within Ambedkarite circles in Odisha have increasingly focused on what many describe as “mixed marriages.” The term refers to weddings that identify themselves as Buddhist while simultaneously incorporating rituals and practices associated with Hindu traditions. These include the presence of Brahmin priests, Sanskrit mantras, fire rituals, dowry exchanges, and engagement or practices such as kanyadaan and the symbolic “gift of the daughter.” In many marriages, families also continue to rely on astrology through kundali matching and the selection of an auspicious muhurat, practices that shape ideas of compatibility, timing, and ritual legitimacy. Ambedkarite activists and commentators often criticise these practices because they reproduce Brahmanical structures of caste, thereby weakening the emancipatory potential of Buddhist marriage. Such critiques frequently draw upon Ambedkar’s analysis of caste, endogamy, and the social regulation of marriage, and emphasise that ritual reform is central to the broader project of annihilating caste.

However, contemporary discussions also reveal an important asymmetry. While explicitly Hindu ritual elements are strongly criticised, other practices common within Ambedkarite weddings receive little scrutiny. One such practice is the baraat, the celebratory procession in which the groom travels to the bride’s home accompanied by music, dancing, and relatives. This article examines why certain rituals become objects of critique while others remain normalised within Ambedkarite communities in Odisha. I argue that critiques of “mixed marriage” tend to focus on …
sourceTags: Ambedkarite Communities; Buddhist Marriage; Status Matching; Baraat; Caste; Endogamy

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Media community faces killings, weaponization of laws under Marcos Jr.
content:
A placard highlighting a call to stop the attacks against community journalists placed on the floor during a protest action at the UP College of Media and Communication on May 2, 2025, a day before World Press Freedom Day. Photo by Alex Culla/Bulatlat

“Protecting press freedom is a shared responsibility. Without it, the public’s right to know and the foundations of democratic society are at risk.”

CAGAYAN DE ORO — Four years since Ferdinand Marcos Jr. assumed the presidency, press freedom violations continue.

Eleven journalists and media workers were killed under his administration, according to the National Union of Journalists of the Philippines (NUJP), although two of them were initially reported as not work-related. The latest case happened in May when Nestor Micator , radio broadcaster of D’Empire Radio, was shot dead by an unidentified assailant in Malidegao town which is under the Special Geographic Area of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).

Community journalist RJ Nichole Ledesma was also killed during a military operation in Toboso, Negros Occidental, in April. He was reportedly in the area doing community work. However, the Philippine Army stressed that he was a New People’s Army (NPA) combatant, a claim assailed by media and human rights organizations.

Roxas City-based broadcaster Jay Lavapiez , meanwhile, encountered a near-death experience after he was ambushed in June.

In May, the Presidential Task Force on Media Security (PTFoMS) and the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) signed a memorandum of agreement (MOA) for what they called stronger collaboration and case buildup efforts.

PTFoMS also signed a MOA with the Commission on Human Rights (CHR) last year. Aside from advocating to expedite the resolution of cases, the agreement would establish a rapid response mechanism, psychosocial assistance for victims, and capacity-building and prevention for media workers.

The Philippine National Police (PNP), in partnership with PTFoMS and other government agencies, launched the PNP Media Security Vanguards program aimed at enhancing the safety and security of media practitioners.

Read: Media groups decry harassment of journalists, activist during protest

The NUJP, however, stressed that the State has failed to bring to justice the masterminds behind these killings. Among them were the murders of Renato Blanco, Percival Mabasa , Cresenciano Bundoquin , Juan Jumalon, Juan Dayang , Erwin Segovia , Noel Samar , and Julito Calo . “While four suspects behind two of these killings have been arrested, no mastermind has been brought to justice,” NUJP said in an earlier statement.

Read: Philippines remains dangerous for journalists

The group backed the proposal of Special Rapporteur on Freedom of Expression and Opinion Irene Khan for the Philippine government to establish a “Special Prosecutor” for crimes against journalists and human rights defenders.

On the other hand, the local press freedom group also monitored the filing of cases against journalists and media workers. Aside from libel and cyberlibel, the Data Privacy Act and unjust vexation were reportedly weaponized as a usual form of retaliation against the media community.

Bacolod-based journalist Marchel Espina surrendered to the authorities upon learning that there was an arrest warrant issued against her for an unjust vexation case which stemmed from an opinion piece published in SunStar Cebu in 2024 when she was still the editor-in-chief.

The same charges were filed against Negros Occidental-based journalist Erwin Delilan in the first quarter of 2026 after the complainants got annoyed with his Binalaybay —a term used for Hiligaynon poems—commentaries on social media. Delilan was arrested twice prior to posting bail.

Lavapiez and his wife, India , who is also a radio broadcaster, also faced multiple cyberlibel cases filed by local officials. In August 2025, the Sangguniang Bayan of Sigma declared the two personas non grata for allegedly disseminating false and misleading information.

Cases of alleged violation of the Data Privacy Act were also filed against the late DZRH reporter Misael Gonzales Jr. after publishing the details indicated in an arrest warrant, as well as iFM Cagayan de Oro News Director Menzie Montes for posting screenshots of her conversation with a local official.

The NUJP monitored 15 libel and cyberlibel cases and 17 other forms of judicial harassment so far. These formed part of the overall …

author: anred
title: Rosario: reclaman justicia por el travesticidio de Gaby Banach
content:
Organizaciones travestis y trans de Rosario convocan este jueves 13 de agosto a las 11:30 frente a la Sede de Gobierno, en Plaza San Martín, para reclamar justicia por Gabriela “Gaby” Banach, militante histórica del colectivo Travesti Trans de Rosario. Señalan la responsabilidad del Estado provincial y municipal y exigen políticas públicas sostenidas frente a la violencia, la salud mental y los consumos problemáticos.

Por ANRed


La comunidad travesti y trans de Rosario se moviliza este jueves para reclamar el esclarecimiento de la muerte de Gabriela Banach, conocida como Gaby, militante histórica del colectivo Travesti Trans de Rosario. La convocatoria será a las 11:30 frente a la Sede de Gobierno, ubicada en Plaza San Martín.


Desde la organización convocante sostienen que las omisiones del Estado provincial y municipal, la falta de políticas públicas en materia de salud mental, las situaciones vinculadas al consumo problemático y la habilitación de discursos de odio conforman un contexto de violencia que, según denuncian, tuvo consecuencias fatales para Gaby Banach.


“Las omisiones del Estado Provincial y Municipal, la falta de políticas públicas en salud mental, consumo problemático y la habilitación de los discursos de odio, mataron a Gabriela Banach”, expresaron desde el colectivo Travesti Trans Rosario.


La movilización busca reclamar el esclarecimiento de lo que la organización define como el travesticidio de Gaby Banach, además de exigir la implementación de estrategias y dispositivos estatales efectivos que tengan continuidad en el tiempo.


“Los cuerpos siempre son los nuestros y el Estado es responsable”, señalaron desde la convocatoria.


La concentración también apunta a interpelar a los gobiernos provincial y municipal para que adopten políticas públicas capaces de abordar de manera integral las situaciones de vulnerabilidad que atraviesan las personas travestis y trans, particularmente en materia de salud mental, consumos problemáticos y prevención de las violencias.


Desde la organización convocaron a los medios de comunicación y a la sociedad en general a acompañar la jornada y sostener el reclamo de justicia por Gabriela Banach.

author: TGEU
title: Central Asian lawyers and activists unite for TGEU’s trans rights training
content:
The two-day training in July 2026 aimed to strengthen participants’ knowledge and practical skills in strategic litigation and the use of international human rights mechanisms. It combined legal capacity-building, sensitisation on trans issues, regional networking and peer learning, creating a space where lawyers and activists could jointly develop approaches to advancing trans rights in their respective countries. 


It brought together 15 lawyers and activists from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan as well as five community organisations. In the future, we envision activists and lawyers from Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan joining as well. 


The training was organised as part of the development of our

Central Asian Legal Network (CALN),

 a new informal regional platform bringing together lawyers, paralegals and trans activists from across Central Asia. The trainer was Kseniya Kirichenko (she/her) and the event was co-financed by TransCoalition.


Photo description: Participants during various training activities


Purpose of the training


The primary goal of the training was to ensure that participants were motivated and prepared to engage in strategic litigation for the rights of trans people and to understand the legal, practical, and political dimensions of strategic litigation. The training also outlined the respective roles of lawyers, paralegals, activists, TGEU, and international human rights mechanisms in advancing trans rights across different Central Asian countries.


Key takeaways


A clear outcome of the training was the raising of awareness among lawyers, leading to a greater and better understanding of gender issues and the link between anti-trans initiatives and the broader attacks on democracy and the rule of law.


Another important outcome was inspiration: a participating paralegal said that she had been considering ‘relevant’ education, but the training inspired her to apply to study law at university.


One lawyer decided to submit an alternative report immediately upon learning about the deadlines and a country-specific case concerning an underage trans woman. 


Participants and TGEU agreed on specific activities for CALN over the coming months, including meetings with special rapporteurs, training sessions with overseas legal clinics, peer learning and reporting. We have yet to fully evaluate the positive outcomes of this work, but the fact remains that this is only the beginning of a long and inspiring journey.


“The state, not only in Central Asia but around the world, instrumentalises fear. Fear can be very easily fueled by hatred — it is easy to stir this emotion in people, but very difficult to extinguish it once it takes hold.


We have a serious task ahead of us: to reshape society’s attitudes toward trans people and human rights — to start from hope and the affirmation of equality, rather than pity and condescension.”


– Tatiana Chernobil (she/her), lawyer, Kazakhstan


Your support makes change possible


We work across Europe and Central Asia to advance trans rights, build strong communities, and drive change through research, advocacy, and community-building.


Your donation helps us continue this vital work — defending trans lives, amplifying trans voices, and advocating for justice every day.

Shakti se nutre de las voces de mujeres agricultoras orgánicas del movimiento Mahila Anna Swaraj (MAS) en toda la India. Documenta su resiliencia y determinación como guardianas y protectoras de la libertad de las semillas, y como cultivadoras de jardines de esperanza, un paradigma para la salud y la seguridad alimentaria. 


Comparte sus historias sobre cómo han desarrollado formas de agricultura sostenibles e indígenas que han combatido el legado de deuda y tragedia creado por las corporaciones de transgénicos, y han guiado a sus comunidades a través de los desafíos e incertidumbres de la pandemia.


Este cortometraje de 35 minutos es una ventana al trabajo de base de Navdanya y Mahila Anna Swaraj, sembrando un paradigma orgánico, liderado por mujeres, para nuestro futuro alimentario.


SOBRE LOS DIRECTORES


Neel Chaudhuri es dramaturgo, director de teatro y cineasta radicado en Nueva Delhi, cuyo trabajo explora la justicia climática, la ecología y la agricultura sostenible en colaboración con comunidades agrícolas locales. Entre sus documentales con Navdanya se encuentra Shakti, sobre colectivos de mujeres agricultoras y la libertad de semillas en toda la India.


Yashas Chandra es director de fotografía y cineasta, cuyo trabajo se centra en la India rural, el conocimiento indígena y la resiliencia ecológica. Ha colaborado con Navdanya en cortometrajes que documentan la agricultura orgánica, la diversidad de semillas y las respuestas comunitarias a las crisis climáticas y agrarias, entre ellos Shakti.

title: L'institut Iliade, Bolloré, Stérin et Křetínský attaquent en meute le Planning Familial
content:
Texte paru dans le numéro 1885 du magazine mensuel de la Fédération Anarchiste (

FA

) «

 

Le Monde Libertaire

 

» sur les attaques médiatiques contre le Mouvement Français pour le Planning Familial (

MFPF

) orchestrées notamment par Marianne, Valeurs Actuelles, Franc-Tireur, Charlie Hebdo et les médias du groupe Bolloré.


Le 11 avril 2026 s'est tenu à la Maison de la Chimie dans le 7

e

 arrondissement de Paris le colloque de «

 

l'institut Iliade pour la longue mémoire européenne

 

». Les «

 

libertés

 

», présentées comme le thème central du colloque, ont donc servi ce jour-là à réunir des figures de l'extrême-droite comme Laurent Obertone, créateur du vrai-faux magazine satirique La Furia et Alice Cordier, cheffe du collectif Némésis. Le 70

e

 anniversaire de l'association du Mouvement Français pour le Planning Familial (

MFPF

) sert aussi de carburant aux paniques morales habituelles des médias du groupe Bolloré comme CNews ou le Journal Du Dimanche (

JDD

).


«

 

Liberté

 

», «

 

Europe

 

», «

 

Destin

 

» ou encore «

 

Civilisation

 

» : autant de termes mobilisés par l'institut «

 

Iliade pour la longue mémoire européenne

 

» le 11 avril 2026 à la Maison de la Chimie dans le 7

e

 arrondissement de Paris. À deux pas de l'Assemblée Nationale, cette association héritière de la Nouvelle Droite (

ND

) et du Groupement de Recherche et d'Études pour la Civilisation Européenne (

GRECE

) a donc réuni à l'occasion de son 13

e

 «

 

colloque

 

» annuel toute une panoplie de figures d'extrême-droite comme Laurent Obertone, créateur avec Marsault et Papacito du pseudo-magazine La Furia et Alice Cordier du collectif Némésis. Le plus ancien de tous ces «

 

activistes

 

» présent dans les mouvements nationalistes depuis la fin des années 60, Jean-Yves Le Gallou, était évidemment de la partie. Sa fondation Polémia qu'il a créée en 2002 organise aussi des événements presque annuellement comme le «

 

Forum de la Dissidence

 

» ou les «

 

Bobards d'Or

 

» dont l'édition 2026 a été retransmise en direct par le «

 

média

 

» Frontières qui avait pour l'occasion envoyé l'une de ses têtes d'affiche, Louise Morice.


Une nébuleuse ancienne proche de La Manif Pour Tous


La Manif Pour Tous (

LMPT

), qui s'est illustrée en 2012 et 2013 par sa lutte contre l'ouverture du mariage aux couples homosexuels, a entraîné dans son sillage la formation de nombreuses organisations. Parmi elles, on peut citer «

 

Les Antigones

 

», collectif identitaire que l'on peut considérer comme les ancêtres de Némésis. «

 

Les Antigones

 

» a ainsi été fondé par des militantes issues d'une scission de l'organisation royaliste «

 

l'Action Française

 

» et du club de scoutisme de la

ND

 baptisé «

 

Europe Jeunesse

 

».

LMPT

 semble dans ce cadre avoir permis aux Antigones d'amorcer une dynamique que l'on peut retrouver à la fois dans Némésis et à la fois dans l'environnement de la

ND

 comme l'institut Iliade.


Par exemple, la présidente des Antigones Anne Trewby est interviewée le 19 février 2024 sur le site d'extrême-droite Breizh-Info par Audrey d'Aguanno, participante à l'édition 2023 du colloque de l'institut Iliade. Anne Trewby affirme ainsi que «

 

le patriarcat n'existe pas

 

» et que l'unité du corps national doit être «

 

fondée sur la cellule de base qu'est la famille (et donc le couple)

 

»

 [

1

]

. En 2023,

LMPT

 change de nom et s'appelle désormais le Syndicat de la Famille (

SF

).


Sa présidente depuis 2013 s'appelle pour sa part Ludovine Dutheil de la Rochère et vient de la Fondation Jérôme Lejeune, opposée depuis sa création en 1995 à l'Interruption Volontaire de Grossesse (

IVG

). Le 9 mars 2026, elle déclare dans un article du Journal Du Dimanche (

JDD

), propriété du groupe Bolloré que le Mouvement Français pour le Planning Familial (

MFPF

) qui fête en 2026 son 70

e

 anniversaire ignore les femmes qui veulent s'occuper de leurs enfants.


Le groupe Bolloré joue évidemment un rôle majeur dans le développement de ce type d'idées. On peut citer à titre d'exemple le passage non annoncé du film «

 

Unplanned

 

» sur son ancienne chaîne C8 juste avant de cesser définitivement d'émettre le 28 février 2025. Ce film, déjà diffusé en 2021 par la même chaîne, dénonce ouvertement l'avortement et est arrivé sur le marché français de la vidéo à la demande du fait de la société

SAJE

 Distribution. Cette entreprise a de son côté …

author: S. Baum
title: Michigan Could Elect Openly Trans Woman to State Legislature for the First Time
content:
Joanna Whaley won her primary, despite her opponent using an anti-trans maneuver to try to disqualify her.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation .

Michigan is on track to welcome its first openly transgender woman to serve as a state representative.

Erin in the Morning readers likely first met Joanna Whaley in April or May of this year, when we reported that the 38-year-old hospital chaplain was running to be the state representative in Michigan’s 2nd House District. She had been temporarily knocked off the ballot because her opponent in the Democratic primary, Frank Liberati, contested her eligibility, arguing her name change documents were invalid and therefore disqualifying.

This maneuver didn’t work. Whaley beat Liberati and one other opponent in the Aug. 4 primary with 56% of the vote, with the second-place candidate trailing over 20 points behind. It was a margin of victory that surprised even Whaley. Now, Erin in the Morning can re-introduce her as the official Democratic nominee for Michigan’s 2nd House District.

She will face off against Republican Ronald Kokinda. But this district leans Democratic, making Whaley the predicted winner of the general election this November. If she crosses that finish line, she will be the first transgender woman to serve in the Michigan Legislature.

While equal rights for transgender people remains a priority, Whaley emphasized that she hopes to represent all constituents. She is campaigning primarily on issues like cost of living, health care access, and public safety. She also denounced corporate money and Christian nationalism as key culprits behind America’s democracy in decline.

“I had a pastor who would, from the pulpit, would say, if you listen to anything other than Fox News, you’re letting the devil into your house,” she told Erin in the Morning. “As a pastor myself, I think that is a terrible, terrible mistake to let a pastor think for you.”

The seat Whaley seeks is currently held by Democratic Rep. Tullio Liberati, the brother of Frank Liberati, who tried to get Whaley booted from the ballot. The current representative, Tullio, was one of eight Democrats who crossed party lines to vote in favor of a resolution calling upon the Michigan High School Athletic Association to discriminate against trans people.

Whaley faces unique obstacles that cisgender candidates may not. In addition to opponents trying to weaponize name and gender marker changes for political gain, trans people are plagued by an endless stream of questions about “electability.” In New Hampshire, for example, State Rep. Alice Wade recently said she was pressured not to run for higher office by a fellow Democrat who cast doubt on whether a trans woman could win in their state.

“I just remember standing in the poll lines,” Whaley said, recounting the primary. “Trans person after trans person, parents of trans kids — coming up to me and saying, ‘You’re making us feel like we can come out of our house again.’”

Meanwhile, Whaley said one of her highest campaign expenses was a security detail due to the sheer volume of anti-trans threats of violence that she receives.

But she credits her time in seminary and the two decades she spent at an evangelical megachurch — an experience that included surviving coercive anti-LGBT conversion therapy — with giving her a unique ability to connect with voters across backgrounds. “I speak fluent Republican,” she told Erin in the Morning. The proud parent added: “The term ‘family’ does not belong to conservatives.”

She admits change will take time, but she said she’s ready to be part of that process. “I don’t think I’m going see the fruits of some of this labor,” Whaley explained. “But it’s just continuing to be that voice of, you know, letting someone’s grandmother hear: ‘Oh my gosh, this trans person talked about something I never thought they would. They talk about loving their family. I thought Fox News told me they hated family.’ I think that that stuff’s gonna matter in the long term.”

Whaley said she will not back down in the fight for civil rights, including those of trans Michiganders. “I’m going to go into the belly of the beast for you,” she said.

Although many outlets are reporting that she will be the first transgender representative there, period, Rep. Emily Dievendorf, of the 77th House District , is nonbinary, and has served since 2022 …

author: Hilmelda Tenkeu
title: Between feminism and pan-Africanism
content:
I read the draft

African Charter on Family, Sovereignty and Values

 the way you read a letter from someone you used to trust. For pages, I was nodding, smiling even. Then I reached my own body on the page, and I understood what the document had done: it had stapled together two tenets of my life that I thought could complement each other, so that to keep one I would have to surrender the other. I always thought my Pan-Africanism gave context and legitimacy to my feminism. This charter disagrees with that.

I am a Pan-Africanist. I am also a feminist. The charter is built so those two cannot share a room.

Let me tell you about the part that got me. When the charter talks about food, it is right. Article 8 asks African states to protect indigenous seeds, to refuse uncontrolled genetically modified seed, to stop criminalizing the farmer-managed seed systems that have fed this continent for millennia, and to put real money — 10 percent of agricultural spending — behind them. When it talks about natural resources, it is right again: removing tariff and non-tariff barriers to intra-African trade to address instability and slow economic growth, no more shipping out raw and buying back finished. Article 9 names the debt trap and our dependence on selling unprocessed commodities. Even its complaint about how treaties get made — the late-night sessions, the documents dumped on delegations in languages and timeframes designed to exhaust them — describes something

I have watched happen to African diplomats

. On seeds, on minerals, on debt, on the right of Africa to decide for Africa, the charter says things I have spent my life saying.

And then it reaches for my womb, and the same word “sovereignty” turns into a leash.

Article 4 instructs governments to “identify and repeal” any legal instrument that, by its own narrow definition, “undermines the family,” and then names what must go: abortion rights, the legalization of prostitution, the “autonomous sexual rights of minors,” anything it files under “gender ideology,” the “LGBT agenda.” Article 7, while championing the preservation of African health and traditional healing knowledge, reaffirms there is “no international right to abortion” and tells states to reject every reference to sexual and reproductive health in every agreement they touch. Read plainly, that is an instruction to

gut the Maputo Protocol

, the

African Union’s own instrument

, which lets a woman end a pregnancy that came from rape or incest, or one that will kill her mentally, financially, or physically. The charter defines marriage as a man and a woman in every legal document, gender as male or female and nothing else. This is not the protection of the African family. It is the government of African bodies.

So here is my problem, and I am not going to pretend it away: I want seed sovereignty, data sovereignty, and the Maputo Protocol. The charter tells me I cannot have all three. I do not accept the premise.

It is worth saying who is holding the staple. A document that accuses sexual and reproductive rights of being a “stealth recolonization” was drafted alongside

Family Watch International

, an Arizona outfit the Southern Poverty Law Center designates a hate group, whose president trains African legislators to lobby at the UN. It was championed from a State House by a president who has built his late career on the

export of anti-gay law

. And in its own final article, the charter lists its inspiration: the

Geneva Consensus Declaration

, the Pompeo/Trump-era American project whose “no international right to abortion” line it copies almost word for word. This is a declaration that Cameroon, my country, along with Uganda, Senegal, Benin, and others, all signed. The thing telling me my health is a colony is itself the import.

L’ironie du sort

, as francophones would say.

20 governments adopted the charter in Accra

; South Africa refused, saying the text could not be reconciled with its Bill of Rights or with the equal marriage rights it grants its citizens, and it was not the only state to abstain. The full list of who endorsed has not been published. The man who hosted and keynoted the conference, who chairs the Conference of Speakers and Presidents of African Legislatures (COSPAL), the continental body now asked to adopt the charter, is the same Speaker who sent Ghana’s own anti-rights bill back for a tidier revote. When a text that claims to speak for the aspirations of African peoples …

author: ABERRANTE
title: ABERRANTE – Anarchxfeminist library opens its doors
content:
OPENING DAYS SUMMER 26’


Adolfstr./Schererstr. 13347, Berlin


15.08 – 16:00 to 20.00


28.08 – 18:00 to 21.00


12.09 – 16:00 to 20.00


25.09 – 18:00 to 21.00


German and Spanish translation below


After months of intense collective work, we are happy to invite you to the opening of ABERRANTE.


In times when digital isolation and extreme control over public spaces are at the center of the state’s agenda, we see an encounter with books in a library as an encounter with others. An encounter with different ideas. We hope that the library will grow into a space of constant exchange, and that moments of self-reflection will also be moments of connection with others.


That is why, from the very beginning, we have invited you all to help build this library collectively by donating books. We hope that every book in the library will serve as a means to challenge our comfort zones, to engage in self-criticism, and to sow new fields of thistles.


Like any large city, Berlin tends to give rise to separatist tendencies and to define centers where much activity is concentrated. When we think of political spaces and events, the vast majority takes place in just a few neighborhoods, of which Wedding is not necessarily one. However, Wedding is a neighborhood where many feminists live in, and projects take place. Opening a library here means building solidarity from the private, reclaiming public space, and reshaping the political through meeting each other. Berlin is home to a wide range of feminist struggles, and we would like ABERRANTE to serve as an excuse to come together despite the alienating dynamics that this city tries to impose on us.


Here we see the potential of a neighborhood that still has a vibrant social fabric. A working-class neighboorhood where solidarity and anarchxfeminist ideas take on meaning through building connections, inhabiting our everyday spaces, and self-defending against patriarchy.


We see ourselves as anarchxfeminists today, building on past struggles and histories that still feel present. We do so by engaging in discussions about our disagreements. Above all, we would like to build ourselves as part of the existing social fabric. For this reason, we envision the Library as a space for coming together. A place where other complicities and affinities can emerge. A place where labels or broad terms are not a tacit agreement but rather a constant collective effort reaffirmed through practice, mutual care, and everyday solidarity. We find ourselves belonging to that part of society that is deemed “other,” that is alien to power, that is understood as ABERRANTE.


In that same line, we see ourselves as just one more project among the many (fortunately) that exist in town, and among those that will hopefully come. We consider ourselves comrades of the other anarchist libraries, through our agreements and disagreements. We are grateful for the exchanges that have been possible so far and, above all, for the support we’ve received from those who were genuinely happy to see an anarchxfeminist library come to Wedding.


Not everything has been a positive experience, and even if only briefly, it’s important for us to mention that the last few years haven’t been easy in this city. We’ve found ourselves discussing the same patriarchal ideas over and over again, with some people refusing to acknowledge them.


We don’t believe that ABERRANTE can be oblivious to this. On the contrary, we want it to be a place where there is no fear of discussing anti-punitive feminism. A place where we can address structural issues that transcend us but also include us. A place where we can discuss social dynamics and personal attitudes, with all our contradictions, but without downplaying the former or focusing solely on the latter.


For us, anarchxfeminism is a constant practice. It is care in our relationships. It is understanding differences without competing for positions or places, it is to fight against heteronormativity and binarism. And therein lies our connection with those anarchist or feminist projects and comrades who understand that anti-patriarchal struggles are at the heart of a search for different worlds. That anti-colonialism is the root of our feminism. And that cooperation with the state will never be an option, because the state does not represent us.


Our hope is that the Library will grow thanks to the contributions of everyone who wants to further anarchist and feminist practices of dialogue …

author: ROAPE
title: The homophobia of Pan-African regimes
content:
West Africa has experienced a series of significant geopolitical developments in recent years, with the potential to reshape both its political landscape and economic trajectory. These are, in many ways, years in which decades have passed. Longstanding regimes have collapsed, populations have expanded rapidly, and economic growth has, in aggregate terms, generally trended upwards across the region. Yet these positive developments have been accompanied by equally serious challenges. A persistent jihadist insurgency continues to destabilise the Sahel, military coups have undermined the post-90s move towards democratisation, and regional institutions such as ECOWAS have seen their legitimacy increasingly questioned, particularly in light of the emergence of the

Alliance of Sahel States

 as a contender to the Pan-African aspiration of politically uniting the region.


An increased repression of LGBT+ communities


Among these developments, one particularly alarming trend, and the focus of this submission, concerns the resurgence of legislative and political repression targeting gender and sexual minorities. Recent developments in Burkina Faso and Mali illustrate the severity of this trend. In Burkina Faso, the military government under

Captain Ibrahim Traoré

 introduced legislation imposing a maximum 5-year prison sentence for homosexuality. This was later unanimously passed by his transitional assembly, materially jeopardising the social acceptance and relative safety of a country where LGBT Burkinabés had previously lived without fear of imprisonment (The Guardian, 2025). This change followed a similar law announced by the military government of neighbouring Mali, which also banned same-sex relationships and introduced mandatory 2-7 year prison sentences for an entire community of people, supposedly in the name of defending ‘traditional and moral values’ (Kojoué, 2024).


These developments, while alarming, are not entirely surprising when situated within the broader political context. Both regimes have simultaneously overseen restrictions on political and civil liberties such as the right of public assembly, alongside crackdowns on journalists and dissidents (Hughes, 2025). However, these actions must not be divorced from the context of the ongoing deadly Sahel insurgency as well as the structural economic constraints associated with longstanding patterns of dependency – i.e. Françafrique. As I have outlined elsewhere, if extremism is to be understood as a germ, poverty is the condition that allows said germ to spread rapidly (Doucouré 2024), with said poverty being directly attributable to the persistence of uneven trade dependencies and extractive commerce rooted in colonialism. It is no coincidence that in two of the poorest and most economically exploited nations of our planet, we may observe serious political instability, the rise of military rule, and extremism. With that said, it would be analytically insufficient to attribute the rise in

the persecution of gender and sexual minorities

 solely to military governance or neocolonial pressures. Indeed, the Republic of Senegal offers an intriguing and instructive mini-case study through which we may complicate the easy answers to questions to be asked of this trend. This is a country that, per Regional/Central bank data, attained for its citizens over 85% of the GDP per capita of both Burkina Faso and Mali, combined. Although, like many emerging economies, the material reality of this relatively strong economic performance is deeply uneven, with poverty very much remaining a significant issue in Senegal.


Concerning the rise in homophobic repression across West Africa, Senegal is a useful case study to consider here not primarily because of its economic position relative to Burkina Faso and Mali but, rather, because the country has generally been praised by geopolitical observers for having preserved a ‘democratic tradition’ (Center for Strategic and International Studies,2024); the transfer of power from civilian to civilian has persisted in spite of domestic and numerous regional constitutional crises (Yabi and Holman, 2024). The country has never experienced a single coup d’etat, a matter of significance given that the fact that Africa as a whole has experienced, until 2010, at least 169 coup attempts – with 51.5% ultimately being successful seizures of power (Powell and Thyne 2011, p. 255).


These democratic and constitutional credentials are to be …

author: Soraya Kishtwari
title: NHS Staff Called ‘Dirty Foreigners’ Amid Rise in Racist Abuse by Patients
content:
Staff in the NHS have reported a rise in racism by patients over the past 18 months, a report based on hundreds of responses from medics has found. 


The Society of Radiographers

collected testimonies

 from 381 of its members, who either witnessed or experienced racist abuse at work.


One respondent said staff had been called “dirty foreigners” while others spoke of patients refusing to be treated by black or Asian staff. 


“I have witnessed a colleague being called a monkey by a patient,” said another. 


Paul Awah, a Nigerian-born diagnostic radiographer based in Bedfordshire. said: “Patients claim not to hear what I’m saying, or say they can’t understand me. English is the only language I speak, and I believe I’m clear enough when I’m speaking to patients.” 


Awah, who colleagues regularly call on to assist with cannulation – inserting small tubes into veins – said three patients had questioned whether he had “done this before?”  


Another radiographer told of a patient who complained he couldn’t understand another colleague who had “a mild Yorkshire accent, but was wearing a headscarf”. 


They added: “What upset me the most is it hadn’t been reported to me – I just happened to hear the staff members talking through it. I felt it had happened to them so much that they just accepted it as something they had to put up with.” 


The society said “increasingly hostile public attitudes to race, diversity and immigration” were behind the spike. It called on the NHS to record incidents of racism and monitor how they are dealt with. 


Roughly one fifth of the NHS workforce is made up of non-British nationals, and one in four radiographers registered with the Health and Care Professions Council trained overseas. 


Last month,100 civil society

organisations signed an open letter

 to prime minister Andy Burnham to back a national anti-racism strategy. 


“

We are witnessing some of the highest levels of racist violence, hate crime and division in living memory,”

they wrote.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Reflections on a decade of UK Black Lives Matter
content:
From

Freedom News

 (

09/08/2026

)


This racist violence we experience is an active race?making project serving the interests of capital


Kojo


Black Lives Matter UK was founded by activists who had worked together on previous deaths in police custody, both in the US and Britain.


In the US, it had started as a love letter to Black people in the aftermath of George Zimmerman’s acquittal – who killed 17-year-old Trayvon Martin in 2012 for the crime of carrying Skittles while Black in a gated community.


In Britain our martyr was Mark Duggan, killed by the Met in 2011. We not only remember the anti-Black propaganda about his criminality, how even some radical leftists argued he needed to die, how the army needed to be brought in to control rioters. We remember the public disregard of his and Black life in general. We live with the reality of State harassment and violence in terms of stop and search, legal sexual assault in terms of strip searches. State racist violence is not only structural, it structures the British economy and State legitimacy.


Today, which is worse than in 2011, almost one in two Black children do not get three meals a day. Ethnically Black African children do better than white British children in GCSEs, but are less likely to get a paid job. All of this motivates us because it is our lived reality.


“I can’t breathe” was said 11 times by Eric Garner, a father of four, who was strangled to death, on camera, by a New York cop in 2014. His death sparked the second iteration of Black Lives Matter protests across the US, and in Britain that became the 2014 Westfield protest.


Sean Rigg, who died in police custody at Brixton Station in 2008, Roger Sylvester in Tottenham in 1999. Jimmy Mubenga in 2010. Those names were with us as we decided to form 

Black Lives Matter UK

.


The US has always been used as a way to paint Britain as moderate, because “we’re not like America.” British policing is seen as sensible. We don’t have guns.


So part of the struggle was not only to continue the fight for accountability, but also about how to make these struggles more visible. How do we honour the lives that have been lost, which continue to be discarded by the State? The thing about Mark Duggan’s death wasn’t just that the police were seen as heroic, they were seen as doing what needed to be done. What that says is when you are stopped and searched, or your home is raided on spurious grounds, when children are asked to be undressed in front of police officials, this is for the public good. You deserve this.


And we wanted a politics of refusal.


We came from different traditions. We weren’t all from one Trotskyist group, some were more liberal, I’m from a more anarchist strand. These tensions played out in asking who do we appeal to? In 2016, all of us came to a conclusion on the day after the Brexit referendum, when we saw on the front page of The Sun newspaper, actual neo-Nazis wearing Vote Leave T-shirts celebrating their victory. For us that was indicative of what was to come. A new revived form of White supremacy. Ten years on, you can judge for yourselves if that’s accurate.


So we agreed to protest on the fifth anniversary of the police killing of Mark Duggan. On Friday August 5th 2016, to the soundtrack of Skepta’s Shutdown, we were going to shut down Heathrow Airport, Birmingham Airport, Nottingham Central. With the motivation of Brexit and police State violence. The impunity with which the police could kill and be told it’s good.


We did disrupt these things. We had people ready to go to the media to explain Britain is not innocent. That Britain’s imperial legacy is framed to perpetuate its present, where Black people are systematically discriminated against. Not only in the criminal punishment system but in education, employment, housing, health outcomes. Every facet of life.


The liberal framework


The liberal arguments that we normally hear are around unconscious bias, unintended consequences, the lag of the State to modernise in a multi-racial democracy and as a result, that policies designed to benefit all people have a disproportionate effect on minoritised groups who live mostly in deprived areas – i.e. State violence towards the working class is normal, it just happens to particularly affect Black and Asian people.


We reject this. While it is true that Black and Asian people live in more deprived areas. It’s not happenstance. The way the economy is structured means there …

author: Andrea DiP
title: Maria da Penha, 20 anos: Alta de feminicídios revela fracasso estatal em proteger mulheres
content:
O Brasil segue sendo um país violento, especialmente para as pessoas negras e para as mulheres. Pelo quarto ano consecutivo, o país registra índices recordes de feminicídios e tentativas de feminicídio, de acordo com o

Anuário Brasileiro de Segurança Pública 2026

.

Apenas no ano passado, foram 1.571 vítimas desse crime, a maioria mulheres negras, assassinadas dentro de casa. A Lei Maria da Penha completa 20 anos, mas a violência contra as mulheres permanece como um dos principais desafios na segurança pública.


Nesta semana, o Pauta Pública recebe Juliana Brandão, advogada e coordenadora de Gênero e Raça do Fórum Brasileiro de Segurança Pública. Em entrevista a Andrea Dip, ela analisa os dados do Anuário Brasileiro de Segurança Pública, o impacto do racismo nas taxas de violência, e defende a importância de políticas públicas voltadas à prevenção e ao fortalecimento da rede de proteção às vítimas.

“Quando a gente se abstém de pensar em saídas preventivas, a gente está consentindo com essa escalada”

, afirma.


Juliana Brandão é advogada e coordenadora de Gênero e Raça do Fórum Brasileiro de Segurança Pública


Leia os principais pontos da conversa e ouça o podcast completo abaixo.


EP 228


											O fracasso do Estado em proteger mulheres – com Juliana Brandão


7 de agosto de 2026


					·


				Coordenadora de gênero e raça do Fórum Brasileiro de Segurança Pública analisa as falhas de crimes contra a mulher


0:00


-:–


15


15


Veja mais episódios desta série


Segundo dados do último Anuário Brasileiro de Segurança Pública, em 2025, o Brasil registrou o maior número de feminicídios da série histórica iniciada em 2015, quando a tipificação do crime foi criada no país. De que tipo de violência de gênero estamos falando?


Estamos falando de uma violência que interrompe a vida das mulheres, uma violência que pode ser evitada. Porque o feminicídio, na verdade, é o ápice de um ciclo de violência que se inicia com um empurrão, um tapa, uma humilhação, com a violência psicológica, patrimonial e perseguição.

Essas violências acabam sendo naturalizadas e desconsideradas como tal. Com isso, a mulher vai se sentindo cada vez mais enredada nesse ciclo

, muitas vezes envergonhada e até se sentindo culpada por estar nessa situação.


Porque estamos falando de uma violência que é cometida por alguém que é do círculo muito próximo dessa mulher. Essa violência do feminicídio, que os dados do anuário trazem agora, é uma violência que acontece na maior parte das vezes dentro de casa, entre quatro paredes. Então, o problema está no ambiente doméstico. O problema está naquilo que acontece quando ninguém vê, quando a porta está fechada.


Quando falamos da violência que atinge também crianças e adolescentes, é também praticada por alguém que é do círculo muito próximo delas e a maior parte das vítimas são meninas negras, que repetem também o perfil das vítimas de feminicídio.

 Então, temos um endereçamento muito certo dessa violência, que já devia ser um sinal pra gente, um farol para onde a gente tem que olhar se a gente quer de fato mudar essa essa situação que a gente está vivendo.


Houve também um número alto de tentativas de feminicídio. Quer dizer que há falhas na prevenção?


Olhando para os dados, a gente vê uma escalada. Então, um recrudescimento da violência contra as mulheres, que não se explica tão só por uma melhora de enquadramento penal, mas por uma situação mais geral. Um caldo mesmo de violência que é expresso por um Brasil que é muito inseguro para as mulheres.


É muito difícil ser mulher no Brasil, porque as mulheres são vítimas de ameaça, as mulheres são vítimas de agressão, as mulheres são vítimas de perseguição. E se a gente levar em conta que essa mulher tem denunciado esses preditores de feminicídio, significa que ela vai e faz um boletim de ocorrência. Ali, por exemplo, já seria um momento de a gente dizer: “Olha, essa mulher aqui a gente tem que olhar com mais cuidado, porque ela conseguiu vencer essa barreira, ela conseguiu entender que não é culpada, ela conseguiu entender que não está sozinha. E o que acontece dentro do lar dela é algo que importa para o nosso coletivo. Vamos trazê-la para mais perto, vamos olhar o que está acontecendo, que rotina é essa, que autonomia ela tem, como é que ela sai desse enredo”, que é um enredo que vai, de alguma forma, dizimando as possibilidades de a mulher, de fato, encontrar uma saída.
